div.p: McDOUGALL'S Pategt SELF-RAISING FLOUR iNINIVON. The Examinek Saturday, August 15, 1908. WOMAN'S REALM. SCIENCE 1-cOTES AND NETS.
COMPRESSIBILITY OF ELEMENTS.

A series of researches has been made by Professor Theodore W. Richards, in conjunc- with Messrs. W. N. Stull, Y. W. Brink, and F. Bonnet, on the compressibility of a large number of elements. A very ingenious ap- paratus was devised for making the measure- ments, and the results obtained chew that the compressibility of an element is a periodic function of the atomic weight, and probably associated with the same causes v:hich deter- Mine atomic volume end volatility.
IMPROVEMENT IN. INCANDESCENT
LAMPS.

In most of the present high efficiency lamps filaments of tantalum Or tungsten are being sidestituted for carbon. A further improve- ment has now been effected by using a sub- tone which does not require the, usual high- pressure vacuum. Filaments of helion, as the new substance is called, can be used in Mins without any exhaustion of the air. The exact ompc6ition of helion has not yet been deter- mined, but it is thought to be some new allo- tropic form of silicon. No prepare the fila- ments the ordinary cellular carbon threads are flashed in a mixture of gases and thereby coated with helion.

the sullen roar of the tempest - was a'nigh over, that the =sitter lay in a deep 'sleep -below. He had given Ned the watch strict orders. 'Doant yer say Ibe able to see any- one,' he had said. 'I be .that done I could sleep for- hours.' All on a sudden Ned starts up. It was • uncanny like, he tells us after- wards. Somethin' was on the move, a'comin' nearer an' nearer along the quay,. an' he sees it stop aside our Hope; an' 'then come stealth- ily, all cat-like, across the narrow gangway. •As Ned goes forrard he sees it is a man, white o' face and wild o' •manner, as coMes close up to him. 'Take this to the skipper,' says the man, hoarsely, an' there is a great yearnint in his eyes. 'lt's a treasure;' he says. 'The masther's nri. for to be disturbed,' says our Ned, an' he tells • us later ac how he eyed the small bundle suspiciously, an' spoke rough- like to the stranger,_an' said as how we didna .want suck things, as ill-gotten goods bring no blessia' on them as receives 'em. 'Take it,' arges the other, eagerly, an' like a flash Ned roJegmises the face of him as we'd rescued but a few hours afore from the • jaws o' death, .the man as had been carried up to the hospital, au' must have got away.. "Ned told us after as how he hesitated, an' then a'thinkin' of all the poor fellow had a'sullercd from the slnkin' of his ship, a ,wave a pity. a'took ioid of •him,- an' he •took up the bundle an' bade the other feller him below. Our Ned henna gone down three steps Of tho. ladder when, he 'looks a'round like. 'Step careful,' he said, an' then he found as . the other had a'gone, estealthily as he had .a'come---net a vestige of him Was to he seen, an' we never sot eyes ,on him more ! 'I was that taken a'back, says Ned after, '.that I nearly dropped the cursed bundle. overboard, an' forgettinl the masther's orders I creeps down, sort-like, into the cabin, . lays the bundle just inside the mastber's berth.' Well, sir, the masther ' had alain asleep for many a 'our, when he Moves rest- less,. his dreams butte' a'troubled like, an' it seemed to him as if an oppression had -come Over him. He half raises hisser, an' rub § his . eyes, as he tells us after, an' at first every- thin' seemed, all blurred like, but all on a sudden somethin' in his narrow berth be- twixt him an' the wall became all ahnovin' like, an' a cold perspirsition breaks' out all over him. ." He told us as how, in all the risks that he had run wi' the •boat, 'he had -never felt such creeps like Itfore. He starts up all awake • like, an' finds as how' it's no illusion, the thing is a'movin' over: It was then as how ha a'Shouted to us all. Comin', sir !" we cry lat the top of our voices. as we nearly push _ _

t . footman, all a'smart like, with his white, Iwig an' his braw new . livery all ablaze, skida,, . ,up on the box aside the coachman, an' the prancing bits o' steeds starts off, an' all the folks about, dome rnanin' out of their doors, an' stare a'gapin' down the street. . "•Ould Joe stands at .his door alooking,, too, after 'era. 'ls it Maid Joe?' we ask . our - Selves. He leeks all joyful an' sorrowful like at once. Have We taken leave of our senses, or is it gospel truth? - The old masther has ao, letter in his hand, an' he looks as if ten years - had been a' put on to is life. ' Mates, he :-tt says, as we come up, 'we've .• struggled en -•;: A ()gather all the years agone, through storm - an' shine, an' I sh-ould like you to look at this 'ore note.' We all a'cireled .round, an' didn't we a'staro ! It was from the ould Dowager— her as went there the day afore—only a tit-- hit of of a letter, • but, it had - the crown • thing j a'top of, it in gold, an' it was her leddyship' writm', sure enough, as We'd seen it a score. o' tiniss. It asked for Hope, all humble 1ike,...,.7 an' said as how the carriage ' was sent tcot, fetch her to what would be her future home.- • •-' " The (mid' masther was all strange like— I. be was so proud for his bit of a darlin' ; but ,;;. he was rubbin' his e'en at the thought of her •.: loss at the same time. div.head: SUNSPOTS AND THE EARTH:.
div.p: SUNSPOTS AND THE EARTH:.

- _ _ The Rev. A. L. Cortie, of Stoncyhurst Observatory, lecturing on " Sun- spots, ' drew special attention to the connec- tion betweeeaf sunspots and terrestrial- pheno- mena. The appearance of the spats hod been associate(' by some persons with a great num- ber of things, including higher temperature, barometrical pressuire, rainfall, the number of shipwrecks, bank failures, and commercial prices. He shewed by records that there was no connection whatever between the curves cf variation of sunspots and those of rainfall, as far as the ek.ieen-year periodicity of the former woe coricMled. There was,. however, a longer periodicity- of thirty-three years in sunspots . and of -thirty-two years in baro- metrical pressure in which a relation might possibly be traced; but this required.

div.head: FURTHER LENGTHY EXPERIENCE
div.p: FURTHER LENGTHY EXPERIENCE

to verify. No doubt, however, there was close connection between sunspot activity and terrestrial magnetism, and this the lecturer traced in detail, „Shewing that in the vast majority of instances there was a coincidence between the sunspot maxima and magnetic Storms. In the few instauc.-_,s in which the storms were . recorded without spots, he wag- r6ted that though the latter had disappeared their sites upon the sun were still areas of solar disturbances, from which ultryl-violet nays and minute particles of matter wire'shct forth into spaca, causing ioni.sation of the upper atmosphere of the earth, which, in turn, gave rise to the magnetic currents con- stituting the storm.

IF THE SUN WERE ANOTHER COLOUR. It is amazing, says Science Siftings, to consider the possibilities if the sun were some other colour. If it were blue, for in- stance, there would be only two colours in the world, blue and black; or if it were red then everything would be red or black. In the latter case we should have red snow, red lilies, black grass, black clear sky, and red clouds. There would be a little variety, how- ever, if the sun were green. Things. that are now yellow would still remain that colour, but there would be -no -reds, purples, orange, or pinks, and very few of those cheery hues that make the world so bright and pleasant.

1 Rex paints adorable pictures, an 3 he's an 1 , extremely nice sort of person ; but ha can be .‘ aggravatingly foolish at times, and once he all but'' .. wrecked my happiness by refacing to see that I was ' every bit as much in love with him as he with me. 1 - And that led me to take up a very odd occupation; , Itnel that again placed me, as you shall hear, in ~. 'what I should have thought an impossible positicn . "-that of being jealous cf myself. , •ft_ y people, you see, objected to my caring for 1 because his income was not nearly as big as ‘.,: , 40Ine of his exhibition canvases; and they gave Rex to understand—as one's people can insinuate :',. ' these things without, apparently, suffering any Verukanent injury to their consciences—that I was already engaged to Mr. Scrobv. Mr. &Toby is a . little fat, and a good deal rich, and ever so s -. 'wearisomely devoted to me; and it was not true '' that I was, or ever could be, engaged to him. I took a sudden craze for etching after that day. My disreputable girl-friend did pen-and-ink things for the magazines, and my people gathered—with as little plain fibbing on toy part as possible—that I was taking lessons from her. Etching seemed so much more Irirmless than roost of my fads that they assented without a murmur, and I was free to go up to town every morning. Rex name to buy a flower regularly, and regularly he stopped for a chat. We grew quite intimate, and I began to be horribly jealous cf mys-lf. It was not Dolly Dene at all in whom he was growing interested, but quite a diFe•ent person, who wore an old stuff dress and a whbe apron, and who altered her face to that nothing hut a I rue lover's instinct could be supposed to r cognise it. I don't believe in your lover's instine.s now, and Rex had no business to drop into confidential relations with a girl nho sold flowers in the street. Still, I 2114.4 Dolly Dene, after all. And at times it struck me as being very funny. The end of it was that Rex, very improperly, asked me to lunch with him at a queer little restaurant that lies ;last off Trafalgar-square. And I, very imprg perly, too, eon ented. And we had a bottle of Ch.anti and coin leasteak pie, and a auantity of other delighttul dishes. Rex suddenly grew communicative. Perhaps I had allowed my eyes to go soft, in spite of my jealousy of the young person who was lunching with him. Perhaps my voice forgot to be as different from its old self as I usually contrived to make it. At any rate, he looked very solemnly at me across the table, and I wondered, with a horrible sinking of the heart, if - he was going to lose Dolly Done for ever and ever by proposing to the young person of ill-regulated conduct. "The fact is," he began, aprorcs of nothing at all, "the fact kir you are awfully 'like someone I once knew." _

"La I" said I. "How very sentimental." Rex squirmed just a little, and I blesszd that 'la." I wanted to be vulgar, you see, and remem- bered the useful little monosyllable just in time. There was a silence. "Was she a toff, this girl you knew? " I ventured, -picking a phrase at random. - Again a silence. I saw, es well as could be, that Rex was wishing I wouldn't spcil the whole effect by talking. So I repented me and looked pretty, and said nothing at all. "Your voice, too, has a touch of hers in it now and then," Rex went on Tresently. "And that trick you have of dimpling in the left cheek before you smile." "Talk of the other girl," I interrupted, bruspiely. "Don't you go pnyirg c3rupliments to me. I won't stand it, do you hear?" Rex shivered very audibly. "Have we finished? Perhaps we had better go,' lie said, rising. Wasn't it droll? Poor Rex was quite capable of developing a passion fcr his little floaer-girl, and this made the flower-girl so awfully angry, in between the times she wanted to laugh ; and she was &ever enough to see that by talking English with a cockney accent she could indefinitely post- pone that dreadful offer which would cut Rex off for ever and ever from Dorothy Dene. I went straight to my girl-chum after saying good-bye to my cavalier, and found her curled up in a basket-chair, a pot of tea at her elbow, and the last frivolous novel in her hands. I sat down on the hearth-rug, which is always the most com- fortable seat in a room. I put ray head in my hands and gazed into the imitation coals of k'un'e gas-tire, and tried to imagine they were real. "Fan," I observed presently, "did you ever hear of a boy named Rex ? " Fan yawned with studied impoliteness. "Several times, dear; a thousand-and-one, I should say, on the lowest computation." "Well, you must have the thousand and second ecltion, then, for I want par advice. I'm rather miserable, old lady." Fan sat up in Ler chair. again at Kensington? " "No," I answered drearily; "I only wish he had. He confines his attentions nowadays to a Piccadilly flower-girl:" Fan, a little puzzled, supplied notes of interroga- tion with her eyebrows. "It is this way, you see," 1 went on calmly. "He comes every day to talk to her, and to buy a buttonhole, and to look stupidly sentimental at her. I have watched him for a whole fortnight now, and sometimes lam close enough to hear every word they say." "What do they say to each other? " demanded Fan, beginning to put on her stern look. Fan is rather fond of looking stern when men are in question. "Oh, he says she has dimples like a girl he once knew, and she giggles and says la,' and—and it is all very disgusting, and low, and horrid." "Just like a man!" commented Fan, icily. " You are very well rid of him, Dolly." "Yesterday he took her to lunch," I added, in a reflective tone. "What will he do nest, do you think ? " "Harry her;" muttered my bosom friend. "These artist-boys always wreck their lives for a senti- ment."
"Has he appeared

"Yes, their own and other people's lives," I whispered, Lrokenlv. Then, somehow, 1 laaghed quite gloriously, and Fan looked mystified, and I got up and danced about the room. "It isn't as bad as all that, Fan. I am the dower-girl he talks to, the girl he takes lunching, the girt who says la.' Now what do you say about it ? " After an interval of profound meditation—Fan likes to trick herself out as a wise woman, because she has got quite a wrong notion about her good loots—the oracle spoke. "I am really very glad, Dolly, because Rex is about the only nun-thing I have any faith in a a—and I dida't think all you said could be quite true."
That was all very well, but now that someone had taken up cadges for Rex, I once mpre saw his conduct in the blackest HOE.

"And, pray," I observed, with a vast amount of disdain, "pray, do you think he has behaved as a man one has faith in should behave? Suppose we were married—l say suppose, because I shall never dream of it now—should I have to let Ilex go making love to every wart= who rstuinded him of mo. That strikes me, Fan, as rather too elaborate a .forrn of compliment." "Now, don't skip on to your pedestal, there's a dear. Pedestal-people are always sa unreasonable. It was just, you that Rex grew interested in, though he didn't know that the real you underlay all those little tricks of manner."

"Humph! You are not very plausible, Fan." She thought awhile ; then, triumphantly: "You goose, don't you see that Rex comes out of it with flying colours. Ile is so much in lore with Dorothy Dene that he makes friends with her wherever he finds Ler. Why, if you had been a washerwoman, it would have been just the same." "Not quite ; less picturesque," I corrected. "You can lose him again if you are really anxious," said Fan, severely. "Thank you—yes—l am ,just a little anxious to lose him. My life is done with." With that I kissed Fan a melancholy good-bye, and went down the stairs, and wished that she hada't driven me into such a gloomy attitude by prsstuning to defend the miserable boy. Only, my spirits rose as I ft-A nearer home, and by dinner- time I was almost inclined to admit that my best girl-chum had really a good deal of conunonsense. If I had been a washerwoman! It was a seductive idea, but I dared not risk it.

Veil, the very next day I met Rex at the Chip- penhams', in in original character of Dorothy Dene. lie fought desperately shy of rue, until I took my courage in both hands and made a most nnmaidenly dead-set at him and brought him to bay in a nice little sheltered corner of the drawing-room. gother was not there to carry me off, and we had a long, long talk. Rex was quite the conventional block of ice for the first few minutes, but a few turns of voice and face changed all that. He began to thaw, and I began to freeze. "You left town rather obruptly ; do you always go away without saying good-bye to old—to old— friends," I observed.

"Where was the use of saying god-bye? " broke in Res, impetuously. "Everyone said you were going to marry Sccploy ; 1 wouldn't believe it until—l saw you witlr him tbu.t night. You were etting him hold your hand in just the way--" "Vas I? " I. murmured, with a far-away air. "Perhaps I was tired of refusing him, with no one to suggest an alternative." Rex gripped me by the arm, rudoly. "Look here, Dolly, don't play aliout with a fellow. Hadn't I suggested what you call an alternative ' three times a week at least? So you ere engaged to him ?" "I find it hard, Rex, not to shiver when he makes elderly love to me." . -
The.' delightful, idiotic boy got up from the much, and 1.:1.11ed his arms. and eccwied like tut'

Shall we

; co back to the others?" he said. curtly. "But 1 have not the least intention of marryink anybody." "By Jove! Do you mean that, Dolly?" "Except—ah, well, the one man I might bring myself to:marry goes stalking about a sort of stage, looking ibvions thunder. No, sir, I shall not permit it Rex's•dAnify ;ad collapsed, and he was for- getting that one stall palm-tree is searcelysufficient under the circumstances. "Why didn't I see it all long ago? And to think—Dolly, when is the wedding to be?" I smiled complacently, and pointed •to the other end of the couch. "Your place is there, sir; I have to ask you one or two questioxs before—before I refuse you." "All right. Sail ahead! What do you want to know, Dolly? " Rex was altogether too sanguine; I laughed gently as I thought of what I knew, and what he didn't know. "Did you ever," I began, after a pause, "did you ever meet anyone—after you left us in such a • hurry, I mean—anyone who was at all like me? He changed colour and moved uncomfortably in his seat. 'Why—l sly, Dolly—what makes you • ask such a qaestion ?" "Anyone who reminded you of me? " went on, keeping toy eyes pitilessly fixed on his sunburnt face. "Tl;ore isn't anyone like you in the world," said Rex:, with a gulp. , "No one wtio dimples in just the same way when she smiles ?" He discovered a minute speck of dust on the sleeve of hie coat, and bettoWed a vast amount of attention en it. I was SO gl d that he hadn't the readiness to rrotest, and tell fibs, ,and deny the existence of all other dimples ; and I really forgave Rex then, though I naturally wanted to have a I,ttle more fun at his expense. We sit there for a considerable time, until the silence grew positively oppressive. "Of course, you're a democrat," I remarked at last. "I try to be," said Rex, eyeing me with renewed disquiet. He seemed to suspect the txistenee of a powder-mine just under our feet. "Su it really won't matter that she wears an old stall gown and an apron, and drops an h ' occasionally, and sajs ' la ' when you make pretty ,speches to her? " "Who told you? " he blurted out. "I suppose it was the flower-selling that attracted you That is the worst of being sentimental. Will you paint her, do you think ? Rex looked awfully sorry for himself._ "So it's all up with me?" be muttered. "Just because she was like you, and 'I hadn't anyone else to think about, und--" "So you don't really care for her "1 demanded, with some asperity. I was growing je duos of Dorothy Dene, now that Rex was Fo. eager to dismiss the flower-girl. It is a very strange world, in spite of (lie hest of people who have said the same thing. "Because she is like you—yes." Wasn't it pretty of him? It just came out, withont the least premeditation, and he couldn't possibly have thought out a better thing to say. The flower-girl 'and Dolly Dene were reconciled, and the sooner they both got engaged to the boy who deserved neither—well, the bettkr it would be for their joint peace of mind. "Rex," I said, very softly. "Yes? "

"Perhaps—l'm behaving generously, I know— primps you had better marry the girl in the apron. he has bten a very good friend to me, and I know she is dreadfully fond of you, and—she will meet you in the Green Park at eleven to-morrow morning. La, la, la I" Fel looked at me in a puzzled way, and I looked at Res ' • and I smiled impertinently, just so that I could bring out that little nest of dimples in the left cheek. Then the silly boy's face cleared, and I never in all my life saw anyone look so happy. "I said I was an ass, Dolly. To think of my never guessing! So I can marry you both?" "That altogether depends, sir. The flower-g'rl will marry you, I believe, but Dolly Dene is by no means sure about it. You must give her time to think it out." . .

• ..... "I'll do that," laughed 4ex: "I'll give her, exactly ten seconds." And then I had to explain, gently but firmly, that one small palm is really a very insufficient screen for that kind of thing. And I believe OM hostess saw us. And I don't care if she did, becau e both of us are going to Marry Rex. [THE END. •

div.head: BUTTER FROM A TREE.
div.p: BUTTER FROM A TREE.
In Ashanti there grows a tree resembling in appearance the Raglish oak, which fur- nishes excellent butter. This vegetable butter keeps in good condition all the year round, in spite of the heat.

div.head: VALUABLE CLOCK.
div.p: A VALUABLE CLOCK.

An astronomical clock, which cost 16,000 dollars, was lately Bresented to King Alfonso of Spain by the Republic of Peru. A figure representing, the Muse of Astronomy holds it. The zodiac, stare, figures, etc., are made of lapis lazuli, gold, and precious gems.

div.head: IRON FROM SAND.
div.p: IRON FROM SAND.

A curiotts sight on the coast of Java is a stretch of shore about 0 miles in length, where the sand is filled with particles of iron. In some places it is said that the sur- face sand contains 83 per cent. of iron. The metal can be extracted and turned to proflt- able account.

div.head: EATC/lED IN EIS POCKET.
div.p: EATC/lED IN EIS POCKET.

From America comes a .very strange story. A farmer, while ploughing with a pair of horses on his farm, turned up a nest contain- ing what he supposed to be turtle-eggs. He put them in his pocket to carry them home. Some time later, when he took up his coat, he felt something moving, and upon investi- gation found that the eggs had hatched and his pocket was full of young snakes.

div.head: SERVIA'S MARRIAGE BANKS.
div.p: SERVIA'S MARRIAGE BANKS.

Servia has its "marriage banks." Early in life young men and women begin subscribing to these, the intention being that by the time they wish to get married a good sum shall have accumulated. The result, however, has preyed to be that large numbers of people rush into matrimony directly a .few pounds have been saved up, and unhappy marriages are frequent.

div.head: mil IN MINES.
div.p: mil IN MINES.

Lehigh 'County in America boasts of the most unique fish culture plant in the coun- try. Years ago, when the failure of Jay Cooke and. C 0.., of New York, closed every hematite ore mine in the county, the pits, which cover many acres of grouna and range in depth from thirty to one hundred . feet, began to fill up with water. One day a boy conceived the idea that these ore mines would be ideal breeding places for fish, so he caught a lot of sunfish, catfish, suckers, eels, and chubs and , dumped them into the waters of the pit and forgot all about it. These fish multiplied with amazing rapidity. Several years later a fisherman on his way home from a ti-out stream happened to pass this particular pit. Merely as a joke he baited his hooks with worms and made a coot. He had scarcely done so when his reel commenced to sing and to his great amaze- ment he pulled out two enormous sunfish. He made a quiet investigation, and readily obtained permission from the owners of the pits to experiment in fish culture. He com- menced to plant black bass and yellow perch. He • went about it secretly, and the owners, who did not want to be annoyed by appli- cants for fishing privileges, also kept quiet. To-day these pits fairly teem with fish.. •

div.head: TIT E TINKEE'S SEAT.
div.p: TIT E TINKEE'S SEAT.

Upon the reading-desk in Swaill am Church, Norfolk, are to be seen sonic qyaint • carvings of a pedlar and his dog, to which is attached a somewhat curious legend in con- nection with the edifice itself. The . carv- ing originally formed part of the Tinker's Seat, so called from the fact of its having belonged to a native named John Chapman, who followed this calling many years ago, and who, it is said, dreamt that if he went to London-bridge he would hear of some- thing greatly to his advantage. Going thither, and after walking about for some hours, he was accosted by a stranger, who told him that at Swaffham, in Norfolk, dwelt John Chapman, a pedlar, who had a tree at the back of his house under which was buried a pot of money. On hearing this the tinker hastened home, and, digging under . the tree, is said to have found two large pots ' full of ruoney. It is with the proceeds of the tinker's strange discovery that the tower . and north aisle of Swaftham's beautiful 1 church are said to have been rebuilt.

div.head: "MAHE PAIRS."
div.p: THE "MAHE PAIRS."

The famous "Shark Papers" are among the relics of national interest supposed to have been lost in the earthquake at Rings- ton. In the.year 1799 Lieut. Michael Fitton of H.M.S. Ferret, was cruising off Port Royal, when his crew caught a big shark. Inside it was found a bundle of ship's papers belonging to an American -brig, the Nancy. Onahts return to Port Royal Lieut. Fitton found that the Nancy had been brought in for carrying contraband of war. Her skip- per produced other papers- to the authorities, which apparently cleared the .ship—false papers, which had been prepared in the event of the vessel being stopped.) Her true papers, which proved that the Nancy was deeply iimVicated in the contraband traffic, had been thrown overboard just before she was overhauled, and the shark had swal- lOwed therh. At the trial Lieut. Fitton ap- peared on the scene, and produced his find, to the consternation of the other side. The shark's jaws are now •in the United Service Museum.

div.head: CURIOUS TUNISHMENT.
div.p: CURIOUS TUNISHMENT.

Above the gateway of Taunton Castle are two rooms in which are stored the records of the manor of Taunton; once one of the greatest and richest manors of England. A number of the manuscripts in the exchequer chamber, which consiSt of rolls -of parch- ment, have recently been examined, with in- tcresting rcsults. The earliest roll that has appeared so far is of Henry V.'s reign, while the first complete roll ,bears the date .1424. One refers to "orders 'of public penance'' imposed on persons for behaving badly in .church, calling each other mutes, and other 'offences. The offenders had to stand in the middle i.le of the church during the whole service and sermon, generally dressed in a white sheet and holding a white wand. After the sermon a full confession had to be made and pardon asked before the whoa congre- gation.

div.head: FAMOUS OLD CLOCK.
div.p: FAMOUS OLD CLOCK.

On the face, or dial, there I are no hands, but in lieu thereof are figures 1 representin,g the • sun, moon, and a ctar, indi- -leating respectively the hour, thc. day of the 1 Month, . and the phases .of the moon: . For - , 1 more tnan a generation the cloak has not Fonc, but there is a prospect of it perform- ing ito functions ere long, thanks to Mr. 1 ' Hill% an expert in horology, now living at Exeter, who has spent many months in try- ing to put it right. . div.head: STOCES IN CHURCHYARD.
div.p: STOCES IN CHURCHYARD.

Not only is the little church of Llandieu, at the foot of the Black Mountain, Brecon- shire, well known to antiquaries for its curious rood screen, but it also boasts of another curiosity in the shape of • a hand- stocks. A high mound to the south of the church is surmounted by a yew tree, through the trunk of which is a large hole. Through this hole the culprit had to put his hands, which were then fastened down on the oppo- site side of the tree by a wooden contrivance which secured the wrists in the same way that an ordinary stocks secured the feet. In this position the offender had to stand in full view of the congregation as they emerged from the church porch.

The KING'S meeting with

OURSELVES the GERMAN EMPEROR at AND GERMANY. Cronberg is being almost generally regarded in this country as the most natural thing in the world, whereas his meeting with the Czar. of RUSSIA at Revel was far and away the most unpopular event of his reign. The contrast in public feeling is, in fact, in masny ways very remarkable. To be sure, the EmrEnon WILLIAM is not banging and banishing and imprisoning his subjects in great numbers : he is not encourgaging bodies like the Black Hundreds ; he is not condoning massacres by rewarding the authors. There are reasons, however, why the meeting of the KING with the EMPEROR might have been regarded far otherwise than with that pleased satisfaction which seems to be the almost generally prevailing sentiment. There has been in England a prolonged and, as we imagine, rather costly effort to embroil us with our German neigh- bours. Germany has been represented to us as an enemy "on the pounce." We have been appealed to as if we were a pusillanimous, and not a brave, people. Obviously, all the scate head- ings" and the scare opinions which accompanied them have been without effect. The people of Great Britain have not permitted themselves to be frightened. They do not believe the scare- mongers. The KING goes to meet the Kenna amid delighted popular approval. They say to the scaremongers what the lady says in the play : "You may talk as you like, SIGNOR BENEDICK nobody marl as you." The fomenting of apprehensions concerning Germany has been a popular form of more or less intellectual recreation for more than thirty yeara past. All men who are past middle ago will remember how the country was affected by the publication of "The Battle of Dorking," which appeared soon after the conclusion of the Franco- Prussian War. GENERAL HAMLEY, the author of that startling work, imagined an actual invasion of this country by Germany, but under conditions that have long ceased to exist. PRINCE BISMARCK laughed at the idea even then. He said that he could conceive of a dozen ways of getting into England, but not one of getting out again. GENERAL HAMLEY'S object in writing "The Battle of Dorking " was partly military but mainly literary. He wished to wake up the War Office and also to write a successful book. He was successful in both his designs, and incidentally he cost his country a great deal of money, as is made apparent by the fortifications which extend along certain of the chalk downs of Surrey. More than a quarter of a century has passed away, and things are as they were, except that Great Britain and Germany are both more powerful for offence. The peace has never even seemed likely to be broken; and yet the cry raised by General HAmLny has been resounding at intervals all the time. There is a small anti- German party in England, and there is a small anti-English party in Germany; and each of these is, to the best of its power, egging the two countries into conflict, fortunately without per- ceptible result, Except in the increase of arma- ments, which in Germany is rather a consequence of Imperial pride than of any idea of preparing for war, and in this country is a necessity of the situation created by the increase of a rival fleet. General Sir ALFRED Tunxxn, who is almost as much at home among the Teutons as among his own countrymen, and whose patriotism and good sense will not be doubted, though he chances to be almost the only Liberal amongst our General Staff, says that the idea that Germany contemplates invading Eogland is regarded in Germany as a silly nightmare. Which is what it really is. One of the scare newspapers put the case hypothetically the other day. It is said that if Germany could land 500,000 men in England, with supplies behind them, the situation would be serious. This is a statement which nobody will deny. It would be serious if the Channel Fleet were to go down in a gale, or if many other inconceivable accidents were to happen. If ifs and ens were pots and pans there'd be no work for the tinker. So the wisdom of our ancestors expressed itself. If Germany had lost its senses sufficiently to wish to invade us, it might have done so with at least a remote chance of success during the Boer War, when it had quite las much, even more, reason for invasion than now, and when the country had been so denuded of / ammunition that Mr. BALFOUR, as he said, could ' not sleep for thinking of the pickle we were in. Invasion was, of course, out of the question then as it is out of the question now. If Germany contemplates anything hostile to us it is rivalry on the saa. She is constantly driving us to fresh expenditure in vessels: but it is merely a rivalry of purses, and ours is the longest. If, in the course of a friendly conversation, the KING should convince his nephew of that fact he will have done one more great service to civilisation.

div.p: ROUND ANGLESEY,

--- - It will be seen from. our advertising columns that the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Co. are advertisin; an Anglesey trip for Sunday next, 16th Inst. This will be the last Sunday voyage of the season, and with fine weather there is no doubt the trip should be well patronised. Special trains are being run from Manchester,and also East Lancashire stations, also special cars from St. Helens and Liverpool outside districts. There will be two more week-day sail ings round Anglesey, viz., Tuesday, 18th, at 9.15 a.m., and Wednesday, September 2nd at 0.15 a.m.

If Warrington Show had WARRINGTON' been favoured with a fine SHOW. day we should have felt there was something new to comment upon, but with the weather consist • ently bad and the show consistently good, it becomes a difficult matter to find any fresh aspect to deal with. o.le fact is note- worthy—that although the climatic conditions were ot much the usual kind, the visitors were more numerous than last year and the receipts showed an advance of £2O. This is an evidence of the interest which the show arouses locally amongst people who, living in a manufacturing town, cannot be said to have any special knowledge of agriculture. Warrington Show is well managed and has built up for itself a great reputation, some of the foremost exhibitors in the country being annually represented. Its horses are famed far and wide and it is doubtful whether this section ever boasted a finer display of animals than those which appeared in the ring at Walton on Thursday. Toe judges were not to be envied in their difficult task of discrimination, for the competition in certain classes could hardly have been keener. S)1110 scribe has described Warrington Show as " the Richmond of the North." It is not quite that, but if it continues to make the headway wdich has so far character- ised its work, the ideal may not be beyond realization.

The sentences passed upon THE MILE END the ten Mile End Guardians SCANDAL. for zorrupt practices were as salutary as the most ardent public purist could have wished. M. Justice Phillimore is a judge of the stern, unbending order where offences against public morality are con- cerned, and he made an example of the Guardians who had corruptly made use of their public posi- tion for the'r private advantage. In summing up the case his Lordship said "that if any of the defendants were guilty the jury would be doing a public duty by finding such a verdict as would, he trusted, tend to stamp out the insidious growth of corruption in local municipal bodies, of which, unfortunately, they had heard a good deal in the last quirter of a century." The jury did do their duty, with the result that nine of the ten defend- ants were sentenced to hard labour in addition to being heavily fined, while the tenth escaped com- paratively lightly with a fine of £250. The names, position, and punishment of the defendants are worthy of 3pec'al note : Thomas Gould, feather dyer, fined £25 and sentenced , to 15 months' hard labour._

Joseph Gilson, butcher, fined £250. Alderman Rowland Hirst,J.P. (ex-Mayor of Stepney), £250 and two years hard labour. Walter Trott, greengrocer, John Edward Loftus, tailor, Archibald W. A. Ridpath, John Frederick Stammers, Samuel Gilder, secretary ; all fined £25 and nine months' hard labour. Alderman J. G. Warren, J.P., grocer, £250 and twelve months hard labour. John Edward Kemp, £25 and sic months hard labour. According to "The Times" the practices of the prisoners have not been peculiar to them, but that between thirty and forty guardians or offl:ials of parishes in the Eipt End of London have been during the past two years found guilty of similar offences. This is a sad reflection on our boasted municipal government. The Mile End case will doubtless cause much searching of heart and conscience in every municipality in the country. Men are prone to err, especially when the way is easy and the profits substantial, as they were at Mile End. Hera in Warrington, the fate of the culprits cannot fail to induce reflection. We have had our scandals—a Councillor has been fined £lOO and a ratepayer disfranchised, while other men have done things which earned them the condemnation of their fellows even if they escaped appearing before a judge and j try. While it would be unjust to generalise from the cases under notice, or conclude that the honesty of public bodies is declining, yet there is much room for improvement. The law requires amending, so that it will be less easy for men to skate round the Corrupt Practices Act. Public spirit is like- wise somewhat deficient. How often do we find candidates for public office carelessly selected, and in the case of Guardians particularly, elected to positions of trust by a mere minority of the ratepayers ? The responsibility for scandals like that at Mile End is largely with the rate- payers. Unless they carry out the duties of citizenship in all seriousness, public ad,ninistration is bound to fall short of the highest standards and may very probably sink to the lowest.

Colonel Richard Pilking- COLONEL PILUING. ton's will comes as an TON'S REMIRKABLE incident that is bound to WILL. attract a good deal of attention in the campaign for and against the Licensing Bill. Although the former Conservative member for Newton Division was known as an advocate of Temperence, we do not recall him as a strong teetotal worker. Certainly, his activity in the House of Commons I was in the main on other lines. In his will, how- ever, he affirms: My experience acquired as a large employer of labour, as Justice of the Peace, and my observation of what is hourly taking place has convinced me that the present facilities for the sale of Moors operate to the prejudice both morally and materially of large masses of the community, and that those facilities ought to be curtailed. Colonel Pdkington proceeds to give effoct to his view by providing that there shall never be any sale of intoxicating liquor on the property which he bequeaths. His remedy is considerably more drastic than the Licensing Bill at present before the House, and we may note that in passing that nobody is likely to contest the right to impose these restrictions, although they are those of a single individual, and he dead. No doubt different persons will draw different morals from the con- trast between the position accorded to one land- owner and a majority of the people.

div.head: -..-e .- THE PRICE OF GAS
div.p: -..-e .- THE PRICE OF GAS
Committee Recommentl a Reduction.

There is good news for gas consumers. At their meeting yesterday the Gas Committee of the Corpora- tion, in accordance with the intimation given at the Town Council meeting on Tuesday, considered the price of gas, and decided to recommend a reduction of 23. per 1,000 feet. This will bring the price down to 2s. 81. per 1,000 less discount.

div.head: COLONEL R. PILKINGTON'S WILL. --- Remarkable Stipulation as to Drink Selling.
div.p: COLONEL R. PILKINGTON'S WILL. --- Remarkable Stipulation as to Drink Selling.

Colonel Richard Pilkington. C. 8., ,of Rainford Hall, near St. Helens, chairman of Richard Evans and Company, Limited, and the Helens Cable Company_ Limited, and M.P. for the Newton Division of South West Lancashire from 189J-190G, left a fortune valued at £692,858 gross and £477,527 net. The will is dated September 7th, 1906, by which testator states :—" My experience acquired as a large employer of labour, and as a justice of the peace, and my observation of what is hourly taking place have convinced sue that the present facilities for the sale of intoxicating liquors operate to the prejudice both morally and materially of large masses of of the community, and that those facilities ought to be curtailed. I direct that any sale of my real estate to my sons and others shall be subject to the following conditions :—That no purchaser, his heirs or assigns, so far as it is within the power to prevent the same, shall allow any building structure or erections to be set up upon any part of the real estate for the sale or con- sumption on or off the premises of any beer, wines, or spirits, or for the purpose of receiving orders, and I entreat my son who may become the purchaser to carry out my instructions loyally and in no grudging spirit, assuring him I have not intro- duced this present stipulation without being fully convinced of the propriety thereof." This condition is made to last for twenty-one years after the decease of the longest lived survivor of Queen Victoria, and the testator states that he would have made it to last longer had the law allowed. He gives to his wife Louisa £5OO, the jewels', wines, Spirits, horses and stores, and the use of his residence land furniture, and the income from £90,000 debentures of Pilkington Bros., Limited. He bequeaths to his eight children various stocks and shares in Pilkington Bros., Richard Evans and Company, Limited, and the Sutton Manor Collieries, and the residue of his estate to his children equally. '

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

We hear that the Bridges Sub-Committec of thek Town Council have been considering the scheme for the erection of a footbridge at Howley and have had tenders before them showing that it is quite possible to carry out the work within the estimated sum of £6OO.
* * * [Jr. Winston Churelfill, last weelc, rendered great help in saving the treasures of a country mansion during .a fire.] . . .

W, inston, unharmed ! Well, let's be glad ! His acts of prowness must be toasted : Fur were be hurt we had been sad, Although he's used to being roasted. "London Opinion." * * * The teetotal conditions in the late Colonel Pilking- ton's will must cause curious reflections in the minds of some of those who were his most prominent political supporters. When the Colonel addressed meetings at Penketh, Sankey and Padgate, the chair was frequently occupied by a well-known brewery official, and he had other friends in "the Trade " at Burtonwood and elsewhere. These gentlemen :will hardly feel pleased that the late M.P.'s last will and testament should des should a blow at their trade. * * * While Mr. R. Pierpoint and Mr. IV. P. Rylands were addressing the Primrose Leaguers at Sankey on Protection, some light-fingered gentry discovered that the refreshment tent was unprotected and helped themselves to about worth of the chief prizes. It is obvious that the Primrose Leaguers are poor folks to teach us how to protect trade when their own treasures are filched from under their noses. There is no evidence that the thieves were Free Traders, but it is quite evident they were not dumpers. * * * At St. Paulinus's Church, Lostock Hall, Preston, improvements are at present being effected in the churchyard. Every evening a number of the congre- gation may be seen busily employed, some stone- breaking, some wielding the pick, and others distributing the prepared rubble over the ground. The work is being done voluntarily, and the rector, Father P. C. Mercer, formerly of St. Mary's, Warring- ton, takes part in it as energetically as any of his parishioners. * *

The " circus " at .lark.-et Gate provided a very exciting turn on Wednesday when a hansom cab horse looped the loop at the expense of Messrs. Smith and Walker's plate glass window. There was a passenger in the hansom when it approached at break neck speed, but just before the finale he wisely jumped out. The horse made rather a gory mess among th tweeds and plate glass, and when sawdust had been lavishly distributed over the pavement the scene was suggestive of the Spanish bull-ring after a kill. * ** The Town Council has constituted itself the Pensions Committee under the new Old Age Pensions Act. Not much can be done at present, but when the application forms have been issued there may be need to extend the Committee or divide it up into Wards. There will be a considerable number of applicants for the State bounty on January Ist, and the claims will want consideration. Of course, after the first year the number of the applicants will be only small and the duties of the Committee correspondingly light.

* * Another of Alderman Bolton's wild chickens has come home to roost. When the Allotments scheme was first launched he said the Committee was spend- ing £2OO in order to provide accommodation for eight persons to grow cabbages. Aready twenty-three allotments have been let, and the Act is proving a boon to local workingmen with a taste for cultivating the soil. The busy colony at Latchford, with its gay tool sheds, speaks eloquently of the success of the experiment. It is now suggested that land should be secured for a similar purpose at Bewsey. The Town Council is showing a commendable desire to provide for the future by securing a recreation ground in Lovely-lane. This is a rapidly growing district, and the way houses are springing up suggests that Whitecross Ward instead of being tthe healthiest in the town may eventually become a congested area unless precautions are taken by the present generation. It is satisfactory to note that the representatives of the Ward have their eyes open, , and will spare no effort to avoid the short-sighted 'policy of the past, which is sadly exemplified by the crowded St. John's Ward with its terribly high death-rate.

• * * A very stout old lady, bustling through the park one sweltering hot day, became aware that she was being closely followed by a rough-looking tramp. " What do you mean by following me in this manner ? " she indignantly demanded. The tramp slunk back a little. But when the stout lady resumed her walk he again took up his position directly behind her. "See here," she exclaimed, wheeling angrily, "if you don't go away at once I shall call a policeman !" The unfortunate man looked up at her appealingly. " For heaven's sake, kind lady, have mercy an' don't call a policeman ; ye're the only shady spot in the whole park." * * * The latest Canadian papers contain anecdotes of the late Sir Rockers Buller. As a young officer he was - stationed in Canada, and it was there that he first made his mark. He rendered valuable service to Lord Wolseley in his march from the Great Lakes to Fort Garry (now Winnipeg) to suppress the rebellion of the half-breeds under Louis Rio!. Buller toiled with the men and en-couraged them in every way in.the hard work of hauling the heavily-laden boats across rivers and swamps. He was so like the rest of the men that one of them once approached him with the request, " I say, mate, let us have a pipeful." Buller, holding out his empty pipe, laughingly replied, "That's just the very thing I'm looking for myself." A correspondent of the " North British Agricul- turist " has discovered a new objection to the Access to Mountains Bill. " A lad and a lass," said the irate hill-farmer who stated the objection, " come up here coortin. She draps aboot hairpins in the grass. A coo eats some o' them an' dees. Whae's tae pey ?" Our contemporary shows that the objection is not so baseless as the non-agricultural reader might suppose. "On account of the large number of hairpins and darning-needlea found in the stomachs and hearts of cattle, and of which we have quite a collection," it says, " we know of several farmers who will not allow a woman to attend their cattle owing to the hairpins dropping out of their heads amongst the fodder.' The decrease in the number of milkmaids has ofteix been remarked upon, but the list of reasons hitherto assigned for the fact is evidently incomplete. * * Looking the pictures of health, our local Territorials returned home on Sunday evening after their fort- night's training under canvas at Knockaloe, Isle of Man. They have had strenuous times, exacting manceuvres under a broiling sun, having severely tested their powers of endurance. A newspaper correspondent who encamped with the Brigade writes: —" The programme of work was without a doubt. exceptionally arduous, and by the end of the fortnigyt the men were beginning to get fed up ' with hill climbing and bog-wading. One rather hesitated to make this statement, but the truth's the truth after all, so let it stand. Whether it was altogether wise to work the men so hard is a very debatable point. Some folk may opine one way and some the other. This, however, is certain that, at the end of the train- ing, every man in the brigade was infinitely better physically than he was at the beginning, and that a few more weeks of such work would make the South Lancashire, or any other Territorial brigade, fit to take its place alongside the smartest infantry regi- ments in the Service. The increase in the stamina of the ihen was most noteworthy." * * Mr. John Burns is receiving the tributes he well deserves for his rigorous handling of the corruptir • that has disgraced more than one public body 13 London. It is evident, however, that the process of - purification cannot end with the punishment of the Mile End Guardians, and the question is raised irt many quarters as to what is to be done next. There is a strong impression (says the London correspondent' of the "Liverpool Post and Mercury ") that coruptioe _ in many forms is prevalent in municipal life to, a much greater extent than most people imagine' Only some of the most glaring cases Dace - come to light, thanks in large measure the fearless administration of the President of the: Local Government Board, and a demand is makirf itself heard for an investigation of the whole system OL,_ municipal government in London by the appoiatines of a Royal Commission, or in some other way. It naas: be taken for granted, however, that the Governmen!' is fully awake to the gravity of the question, and that the reform of the poor laws which will follow the report of the commission will embody avreePil changes in the existing system. The present boat'as, of guardians will disappear, and it is expected they will be replaced by a central authority, suPPL° mented by local committees.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES,
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES,
WIDNES " CiARACrEFt " FINED.

At Widnes, on Aron:day, John Grimes, of Nelson- street, described by the police as a violeat character, was fined 40s. and costs for being druak and disorderly on Saturday night. His wife gave evidence, and said it was her fault that she brought the police. Her husband was not drunh. DRINK AND ATrEqPTED SUICIDa

Michael Tyrell, aged twenty-two, of Mossbank, was charged at Widnes on Monday with attempting to commit suicide by drinking a quantity of oxalic acid,on Friday night, in the bar of the Mossbank Hotel. He had just returned from the militia training, and had been drinking heavily. He was handed over to the care of his mother, who promised to look after him.

INCORRIGIBLE; ANN. Arm Carrigan made her fifty-sixth apnearann a Widnes, on Monday, on a charge of being drunk and disorderly. She was, as usual, very talkative. Major Wareing : What are her convictions ?—Superintendent Strickland - Fifty-six, sir.—Prisoner : More nower to it.—Major Wareing : Are you married ? : Yes.— Ts you husband living ? : Yes, sir.—Major Wareing : Poor soul. A fine of ss. and costs was imposed.
SEQUEL TO A TRAMCAR SMASH. £3O FOR INJURIES.

At the Manchester County Court on Monday, £lOO damages were claimed by Mrs. Louisa Ann Dumbill, of Lord-street, Runcorn, for damages sustained in a collision between two electric tramcars of the Man- chester Corporation.—Mr. Cobbett pointed out that as the Corporation had paid LTO into Court with an admission of liability the only question to try was what the plaintiff was entitled to for the pain and suffering and expense she had undergone. On the afternoon of January 4th last she was travelling in a tramcar in Gorton during a fog when a car corning in the opposite direction entered on the same stretch of single line. The shock between the cars was such that the plaintiff was flung from her seat to the floor, which the back of her head struck heavily. The next thing she recollected was find;ng herself being attended to in a chemist's shop. She was in •bed for about a month, and for four other months was kept indoors unable to do anything. Her injuries were serious indeed. She had concussion of the brain and spine ' • she suffered from headache to such an extent that the doctor feared meningitis, and also from backache ; her eyesight and memory were both affected; and among other things she was a victira of neurasthenia and had lost from two to three stone in weight. for before the accident she was a big. strong, stout and healthy woman. Under these circumstances, seeing that she was not likely wholly to recover for some time, he contended that £lOO was by no means too much to ask the Corporation to pay. The plaintiff and Dr. M'Clelland gave corroborative evidence.

On behalf of the defence Dr. Platt, who said he had made two medical examinations of the plaintiff, stated that the symptons described by her and her adviser were all those of neurasthenia, and expressed his belief that she would get better much quicker as soon as the legal proceedings were over. Judge Parry : And the more she gets the quicker it will be I presume. (Laughter.) The best prescription would probably have been for the Corporation to have given her a cheque for the full amount a week after the accident, eh ? (Renewed laughter.) Dr. Platt. : Quite so. In giving judgment, his Honour said that in these cases the Corporation, acting as the trustees of the ratepayers, did right in contesting claims which they had any reason to think might be excessive. Whether the woman's condition was one of neurasthenia or something else did not matter. Ile knew something of neurasthenia himself and had had to deal with many other cases, but he had never known a case with such serious results as this, or where there had been such actual physical pain and suffering. The expenses were not too large in his opinion, and therefore in awarding the plaintiff £79 18s., with costs, he was allowing Gt) or the pain and suffering she had undergone.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
ACCIDENT TO A BOY.

Edward Forrester, aged thirteen, was going home along with his mother over the canal and railway to Double Locks, Parr, St. Helens, about midnight on Saturday, when the lad was knocked down by a coal wagon belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Company, and severely injured. The police ambulance was summoned and the lad conveyed to the Providence Hospital, where it was found that one of his legs was so badly shattered above the knee that it had to be removed.

div.head: --- DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT PRESCOT.
div.p: --- DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT PRESCOT.

Early on Sunday morning the Prescot Corn Mills. occupied by Mr. J. Garth, was discovered to be on fire, The Prescot Fire Brigade was summoned, but on their arrival the whole building was well alight. A number of police also assisted the firemen, whose efforts were mainly directed to saving the adjoining property, which for some time was in danger. At the time of the discovery there were six horses in the building, and these were removed with difficulty. The fire was got under control about eight o'clock. The whole of the contents of the store-rooms, which consisted of corn, flour, hay, and straw, together with machinery, lurries, &c., were destroyed. The damage is estimated at about £1,500 and is covered by insurance.
DRUNKEN BURGLARS. FOUND ASLEEP IN BED.

. A burglary of a somewhat amusing description is reported from St. Helens, where la the early hours of Tuesday a constable found three men drunk and asleep in Led at the residence of the Town Clerk, Mr. W. H. Andrew. It appears that Mr. Andrew is away on holiday, and the house had been placed in charge of the police. About half-past one o'clock Police-constable Ramsden, on exarlining the house found a window broken at the back. He went inside, and found unmistakable signs that the place had bsen, ransacked. On going upstairs he found three men in bed drunk. Whistling for assistance, Constable Watson and other officers arrived on the scene. The burglars are well-known St. Helens men, and they were inclined to resist being disturbed from their luxurious form of sleeping, but they were taken to the Town Hall and locked up. The details of the affair have caused a good deal of amusement in the district.

Later in the day the three men concerned—Michael ohnson, Herbert Allen, and Richard lierivick—m ere brought before the magistrates, charged with burglary and stealing cases of fish knives, carving knives, electro- plate, liquors, S:c., value £lO, the property of Mr. W. H. Andrew. A week's remand was granted. LABOUR MEETING AT ST. HELENS.

Mr. T. Glover, MX., on Monday addressed a meeting of his constituents at ihatto Heath, St. Helens, and said that the local Labour party desired to raise the interests of the working men of the district in the coming municipal elections. It was important that they should I send to (ho local Parliaments men from their own ranks I who understood the desires and requirements of the , people, and who would, with the olject of benefiting , them, try to carry out the Acts which the Legisla- ture intended for their use and service. Many ' good pieces of legislation were dead letters , because there was no one in the districts affected to see that they were put into force The feeding of the poor school children which was provided for by law, was not carried out in some dis- tricts, but, thanks to the activity of the Labour party in the St. Helens Town Council, excellent work had been done in the town by means of that Act. The working people should study those matters for them- selves, and they should be quick to note who was attend- ing to their interests, so that when the electors came round they would be able to reward or reprove the men according to their works. In the same way he urged the people to watch the affairs of the country and see what was being done for them in Parliament. He claimed that the Labour party had, on questions affecting the workers, succeeded in doing a great deal during the last two years that had been of real benefit. For the first time the people had a party in Parliament devoted soley to the interests of democracy, and it was due to their constant watchful- ness and attention that so much had been done by means of the Compensation Aot, the Trades' Disputes Bill, and old-age pensions for the workers. When the people came to properly realise their needs and their opportunities they. would use the power which they possessed and so improve the position of themselves and their children. Mr. H. Twist, J.P., of Wigan, addressed the meeting, and Councillor A Rudd spoke on local topics.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 15, l9OB.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 15, l9OB.
I EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
MOTOR CYCLIST FINED.

James Harrison was fined 20s. and costs at Newton Petty Sessions on Thursday, for driving a motor-cycle at an excessive speed. The police prosecuted, and Inspector Tunes said defendant was timed over a two- mile course from Newton to Wity.vick, and was found to be travelling at the rate of twenty-five miles an hour. Just at the time Harrison dashed past, without sounding his horn, lit) boys belonging to the Liverpool Reformatory, located at? Newton, were out taking walk- ing exercise, and the consequences might have been serious.

SELLING BAD HAM—SEVERE PENALTY. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Thursday, William Fisher, of Widnes, was charged by the Newton-in- Makerfield Urban District Council with selling 51b. of ham on the public market ground at Earlestown, and which the market inspector and medical officer of health condemned as unfit for food. It was purchased by a Mrs. Lyons, laho has a large family, and after cooking a large portion of it her husband, not liking the smell of the ham, tasted it, and found it abominally distasteful, and did not allow any of his family to touch it or the consequences might have been very serious.—The magistrates said the public must be pro- tected, especially on a market-ground whore goods were sold mostly by lamplight, and lined Fisher .eti and cosets.

HAYDOCK COLLIER'S COMPENSATION. At St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Thomas Hamilton miner, of Penny-laue, Haydock, whose son James died on May 20th last from injuries to the head caused by an accident ia the Old Boston Pit, Haydock, applied for the amount of compensation to be paid to him. Mr. W. Hutchen said that £lOB had been claimed, but £BO had been paid into court, and they were willing to accept it. Applicant asked for the money to be paid out of court. so that he might invest it at a ketter rate of interest than if it was invested by the court. Judge Shand agreed, and granted the application.- -Rose Ann Smith, widow, of Judfield-street, idaydock, asked for £4O to be paid out of a sum of £3OO, which had been agreed as the compensation for the death of her husband, Robert Snith, who was killed on June 27th, at one of Messrs. R. Evans and Co.'s collieries. Mrs. Smith said she had 'four children, but three were married, and the youngest was over twenty-one, and for some years had been keeping himself. She got £l4 from an insurance company, but that " had not buried him altogether," and she asked for £4O to pay some few debts and to erect a tombstone. The Judge asked for bills to prove that £4O was owing, but as none were forthcoming allowed a grant of £lO and £2 per month.
A Lazy Pauper. Edward Oxley, who has been an inmate of the Workhouse since 1903, was sent to gaol yesterday for 21 days for refusing to break stones at tho institution. _

1 A Hackney Pony's Success. At Astley Bridge Show' on Saturday, Mr. Arthur J. Willett's three-year-old hackney pony ,mare, Fire Belle, won second prize in the open harness class, Mr. Watt's six-year-old mare, Mel Valley's Veronilue, being the first prize winner. Councillor Stott. , Councillor Stott, who will•shortly leave for New Zealand, will deliver his final address to the electors of Orford Ward on Tuesday evening in Longford- street (Orford-lane end). A farewell gathering will be held in Cairo-street school on Thursday evening, when a presentation will be made. Local Will

Mr. Christopher Plunkett, of 220, Orford-lane, Warrington, late of the King's Regiment, who died on the 4th of last month, appointed the widow, Mrs. Charlotte Mary Plunkett, sole executrix, by whom the property is returned at the gross amount of .4:831 Bs. 4a. and the net at ..+:812 3s. 3d.

School Girls and the Baths. The Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee have decided to recommend the Town Council to grant school girls admission to the baths on Tuesday and Saturday at a charge of one penny each. At present they have to pay twopence, whereas for some years boys have been admitted for one penny. Change of Inspector of Factories. The Chief Inspector of Factories gives notice that Mr. J. E. Ashworth (in place of Mr. A. Lewis promoted) is now the Inspector of Factories for the Manchester District, which comprises part of Lancashire, viz., the Unions of Manchester Township, : Salford, Chorlton, Prestwich, Barton-upon-Irwell and Warrington. Mr. Ashworth's official address is 72, ' Bridge at., Manchester. Superintendent Monaghan's Retirement. At the instigation of Mr. Arthur Browne a meet- ing was held at the Lion Hotel last evening for the purpose of raising a testimonial to Superintendent 1 Monaghan on his retirement after 28 years service. A large committee was formed with Councillor Singleton as chairman, Mr. Arthur Browne as hon. treasurer, and Mr. J. \V. Millen as lion. secretary. Stockton Heath Football Club. The annual meeting of the Stockton Heath Rugby Union Football Club was held at the Stag Inn on Tuesday eveaing, Mr. A. T. Hallaway presiding. The Secretary (Mr. A. H. Fawcett) presented a satisfactery report, showing that during the season the club had played 23 matches, won 13, lest 5 and drawn none. An attractive programme had been arranged for the coming season. Mr. T. 11. Lyon was elected president of the club,Mr. All. Fawcett secretary and treasurer, and Mr. A. T. Hallaway, chairman. _ _

.„ Nearly Sl,angfed His Wife. At the Warrington Borough Court, yesterday,befora Mr. Tames llepherd (in the chair) and other magis- trates, Richard Mills, 13, Catherine-street, was sum- moned for assaulting his wife, Mary Mills, on August Sth.—Complainant and other witnesses stated that on Saturday night the defendant returned home under the influence of drink, threw her on the carpet, and nearly strang:ed her. Two men had to pull defendant off his wife, and she was black in the face—Defendant, who had a bad character, was sent to gaol for three months with hard labour.

" This," exclaimed the orator. " is a deca- dent nation. As before the fall of Rome every- thing was rotten, so to-day in our erstwhile fair land everything--" Just here an egg struck him fairly. THE MORNING NAP. Lives there a man who has ript said, " To-morrow I'll get out of bed At eix o'clock and get things done Before the setting of the sun." Lives there a man who has not said At six a.m., " How good this bed Does feel." and snored till after eight, Then wondered how he slept,so late.

A Fort Dodge doctor, Dr. X., once had a grave dug for a patient, supposed to be who afterward recovered, and over this error of judgment the doctor 'was joked for many years. Once he attended, in consultation with three confreres, another patient. This patient really died. After the death, as the physicians discussed the case together, one of them said : " Since quick burial is necessary, we might inter the body temporarily. I understand our brother fere has a vacant grave on hand." Dr. X. smiled. " Yes," he said, " I believe I am the only physician present whose graves are not all filled." •

"It is very seldom that they serve actors milt 6ve different kinds of vegetables," whispered the short comedian in the quick-lunch room. "Oh, I don't know," sighed the lanky tragedian. "One time I was served with twenty-five different kinds of vegetables." "You don't say? In what hotel?" "No hotel. The audience supplied them."

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

The Hippodrome is worth visiting this week if only to see Billy French, the stylish wooden shoe dancer. He is wonderfully clever on his feet, and dances in a way that suggests he is enjoying it as much as the audience. Then there are the Gothams, a quartette of accomplished vocalists who combine high class part singing with the comedian's business. It struck us as rather a funny mixture, but there was no turn which received a more enthusiastic encore. Whether the men are singers first and comedians after is a question, but they are equally good in both roles. Personally, however, we would rather they kept them distinct. ,Dave Samuels, the American Hebrew comedian, is also a bit out of the ordinary. He sings and patters in a most amusing way in ' a sort of pigeon English which suits the part, and be is no duffer as a dancer. Dave can also tell funny stories, and they make the audience laugh— which is essential but not always inevitable. A novelty item is provided by Gravetta and Parr. Which is which we don't know, but one does some rapid clay modelling while the other " draws " a sand picture. Then the two combine at impersonating famous personages, such as Kitchener, Napoleon, Lord Roberts, Queen Victoria, and ' were both quick and clever. The lady as the Emperor was specially good. A. really excellent musical act is provided by Les Frasettis, who make most expert and harmonious use of the harp, violin, and xylophone as duettists. Gold and Sterling appear in " The Welsh Girl and the Artist." The lady sings and tho artist paints—a large size water colour of Rocky Mountain scenery being produced in six minutes. Dolly Brough, the juvenile favourite, obliges with a song and dance, but like most artistes of her kind her dancing is a long way in front of her singing. Jim Cheetham, the king of boy whistlers, warbles a selection from the " Poet and Peasant" with orchestral accompaniment, and also gives some clever bird imitations. Why he should deem cricketing flannels, a blazer and white boots, a suitable stage attire is, however, a mystery. We would suggest a Tyrolean reasant's garb as a change. Mr. Widdop's orchestra seems to improve week by week, and some of the accompaniments and selectiots are a musical treat. The cinematograph pictures are also better than ever. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

A capital programme is announced for next week. The bill is headed by Harry Weldon, the swell entertainer, known to fame as. "Stuffy," the goal- keeper in Fred Karno's " Football Al atch." The Waldrons will appear in their original absurdity "The Silly Burglar" and other entertaining features will be provided by :—Renee Grahame, refined character vocalist; Harry Simms, the popular light comedian; Helen Martin, vocalist ; Baker and.Balfe, the versatile xylophone experts (Ur. George M. Baker intro- ducing his famous eccentric dancing with Xylophone accompanist) ; Rose Archer, mimic at the piano ; Fred Carr and Ada Rose, presenting cri3inal operettas.

div.head: WATER POLO.
div.p: WATER POLO.

The Warrington team journeyed to Birkenhead Baths on Wednesday evening to play the return match in the Liverpool and District League. Warrington won the toss and defended the deep end. Birkenhead scored first, and this put the visitors on their mettle, several of the players having very hard lines in their shots for goal, but W. Ashton equalised with a beautiful goal. The interval arrived NS. ith the score one goal each, ' Warrington having had most of the game. Unfortu- nately they lost theservices of W. Ashton in the second half but despite this they combined together and their passing movements were much applauded by the spectators. Birkenhead scored another goal, but the game was soon equalised by Pemberton who scored a brilliant back hand shot which gave the goalkeeper no chance and the final arrived with the score two goals each. If the Warrington team had been at full strength in the second half there is no doubt they would have easily beaten their • opponents. The team included C. Turner tsho played for the first time this season. Warrington, goal : C. Woods; fullbacks, W. Sutton, S. Walker ; halfback, W. Ashton ; forwards, R. Allen, T. Pemberton, C. Turner. The Whitecross team having. protested against Rylands Bros., on the ground of swimming an ineligible man in the Works Squadron Competition, the Committee have upheld their protest and Whitecross will compete in the 2nd round which will be drawn for on Tuesday evening next. The polo will be busy next week matches being played with Leigh away on August ISth, and South Hill at home on August 20th, when a 30 yards members handi- cap will be swam.

RUGBY FOOTBALL. -- Warrington's Prospects. Thcre is not much news tu impart just yet as to Warrington's preparations for the coming season. No new players have been signed on, though negotiations are in progress for one or two likely men. R. Bate, who last season assisted Pendleton,has been transferred to Leigh. It has been rumoured that Harris was going to the same club, but no application has been received for his transfer. No other changes are antici- pated, and all last season's players should be available when the season opens. E. Watkins bus been "on the club " since April with his injured knee, but is nearly strong again. George Dickenson has been appointed captain for the season, W. J. Tilley as sub-captain. Jordan will lead the "A " team.
