A PLUCKY CONSTABLE REWARDED.

The Watch Committee resolved that a gratuity of . RI Is. be granted to P.C. 20 Taylor for mentortous conduct in stopping a runaway horse. Alderman Pt surotsT expressed his pleasure that the gratuity had been granted to P.C. Taylor. lie happened to be in the immediate neighbourhood at the time the accident took place. There was no doubt that the con- stable ran a serious risk, for he sprang at the horse in a most praiseworthy manner and saved what might have been a very serious accident. No doubt the action of the Watch Committee would be an incentive to other mernUrs of the force. SUPERINTENDENT MONAGHAN'S RETIRE- MENT.

Detective-Superintendent Monaghan having given notice of his desire to retire from the police force after upwards of 23 years' service, and the Chief Constable having certified the service as approved service for the purpose of the Police Acts, the Watch Committee resolved: "That there be paid out of the police pension fund to Mr. P. Monaghan a pension for life equal to two-thirds of his annual pay." Alderman Prruporsr, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said Superintendent Monaghan, after 28 years' service, was leaving them. During the whole of his service he (Alderman Pierpoint) had known the officer. He knew him as an ordinary constible, and he had worked his way up to the position of superintendent. At one time he had the entire control of the police force. That was during the unfortunate illness of the late Chief Constable Talbot. During the whole of those 23 years he (the speaker) had never known nor heard anything said against his character as a police officer. He only hoped that the remainder of his life would be spent very happily, and that he might live for many years to enjoy his well-earned pension. (Hear, hear.) A WALKING DAY COMPLAINT.

Complaints having been received of the great incon- venience caused on \Calking Day by the closing of the main thoroughfares of the borough, during the Sunday school processions, the Watch Committee resolved : "That the sama be referred to the Chief Constable, with instructions to report upon the matter prior to Walking Day next year." The minutes were passed, on the motion of Alderman PIERPOINT, seconded by Alderman Eutsox. CONSTABLES AS JOINERS. COUNCILLOR STOTT VOICES TRADE UNIONIST COMPLAINT.

A letter from the Society of Carpenters and Joiners with reference to joinery executed by the police was read at a meeting of the Watch Committee and referred to the Chief Constable. Councitlor STOTT said he had received a similar letter, in which the society complained very strongly about policemen being engaged in what was considered to be joiner's work at the police buildings. He was sorry that the Chairman of the Watch Committee was not present so that information could be given as to whether the complaint was well founded. He had also bad a complaint from the master builders and joiners that there was ft joiner's shop at the police buildings. They did not think it fair to them as ratepayers. Alderman PIERPOINT said the Watch Committee had had the question under their observation. Some little jobs had undoubtedly boon done in putting up a temporary fence, but they were done without the cognizance of the Watch Committee. Such arrange- ments had been made as would, he hoped, avoid any complaints in future. VICTORIA PARK AS FOOTBALL GROUND. APPLICATION REFUSED. The Town Hall, Parks and Bath Committee reporte. that they had received a letter from Councillor XVilson asking for the use of part of Victoria Park for a foot- ball ground. The Committee resolved that at the ' present time they were unable to grant the application SWIMMING ACCOMNIODAFIGN FOR GIRLS.

I The Baths Committee reported that the bath-keeper having reported on the arrangements he had made with the Director of Education with regard to the use of the Baths by school girls, they resolved :—" That the Education Committee be allowed the use of the ladies' i swimming bath during one half-day per week for the 1 sum of £2O, for this year, and that the whole subject be then re-considered," Alderman PIERPOLNT proposed and Councillor EVANS seconded the adoption of the minutes. i Councillor STOTT said the question of providing bathing accommodation for girls was becoming as bad as the question of providing new bridges. The matter came before the Council live months ago, and they were

assured by the Chairman of the Baths Corn mittee that something was going to be done directly. It did not seem as though any accommodation was going to be provided during the present bathing season. The ques- appeared so simple that it ought to have been settled some months since.

Alderman PiEttron-T said the Borough Surveyor informed him that the plans of the new baths were being prepared as quickly as possible, and the com- mittee had not lost sight of the matter. The things could not be done in five minutes. Councillor EVANS said it was a question of whether they could arronge for the girls at the Baths, and he understood from the Chairman of the Committee that tbat was impossible, as the Baths were at present occupied the whole of the day.

THE PRICE OF GAS. The Engineer submitted to the Gas Committee a detailed report with reference to a proposed reduction in the price of gas, and it was resolved that the same be sent to each member of the committee and considered at the next meeting. Alderman PIERPOINT, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said he hoped the committee would be able to agree to a reduction. Alderman PrErtroiNT said a case had been brought to their notice as a wrongful connection to the gas main, • by means of which a man got gas for n,thing. They had a somewhat eimitar complaint a month before, and it became a serious question what to dl in this case. The committee spoke to the householder very severely, and he apologized. He was also directed to pay for the gas consumed and the costs incurred in connection with the case. He (Alderman Pierpoint' 'hrd it to be understood that if any further wrongful connections were found the matter would be placed., in the hands of the Town Clerk for a prosecution. Alderman E:ANS seconded, and the minutes were passed. FIRE3TAN FOR WINWICK ASYLUM'. Upon the minutes of the Water Committee being con- sidered, Alderman EVANs said at the request of Dr. Simpson, of the IVinwick Asylum, they granted the doctor an interview on the subject of having a fireman always on duty at the asylum, and the Committee had undertaken to place one of the men on duty there. The question arose because the Committee had been making re-arrangements of the duties of the stall with the object of avoiding Sunday labour. The Asylum authori- ties were, however, anxious as to what might happen if a fire might happen. Councillor ROGERS seconded, and the minutes were agreed to.

SUGGESTED ALLOTHENTS FOi BEWSEY. Councillor EvA.Ns said it had been suggested to him that he should ask the Chairman of the Small Holdings and Allotments Committee, if a suitable plot of land on the newsey side of the town could not be secured far the purpose of allotments. (Hear, bear.) Alderman FOTISHAW assured Councillor Evans that if application was made to the committee they would give it every consideration. Councillor WILKINSON said only that day Lord Lilford's agent assured him that if application was made for allotments it would meet with approval. Councillor STOTT thought the fact that three more applications for allotments had been granted should be brought to the notice of the Chairman of the Town Hall Committee who repeated on several occasions that the Small Holdings Committee were spending £2OO in order to provide accommodation for eight persons to grow cabbages. Laughter.)( Already twenty-three applications had been granted. The minutes were passed.

PICTURE PURCHASE NOT APPROVED. The following resolution of the Museum Committee ; was read, considered, and disapproved by the General Purposes Committee :—" That the General Purposes , Committee be requested to purchase Brill Brow,' a water-colour, by George Sheffield." COUNCILLOR STOTT'S DEPARTURE. APPRECIATION OF HIS SERVICES. The Generil Purposes Committee resolved :—" That this committee rogret to hear that Mr. Councillor Stott is about to sever his connection with the Council and the town, and desire to record their appreciation of Mr. Stott's earnest and useful services in the Council, and of his iniegrity of purpose on behalf of those he represented; the committee wish Mr. Stott the success which he well deserves in the new sphere of life be is about to seek in New Zealand."

In-n;O-v-ir-illTh.e...a-dOp-tIO-n7i the minutes, Alderman Plum)lxr said as the one who moved the resolution in regard to Councillor Stott, he wished to say that the members of the Council, while regretting his removal from their midst, would like to join in publicly appreciating his services to the town, not only as a town councillor but also as a justice of the peace. They all knew the worth of Councillor Stott, and although they did not always agree with his methods he was a man they would miss. As a representative of his own class and particularly of the trade unionists, Councillor Stott was much to be admired. Councillor EVANS seconded, and the minutes were adwated. Councillor STOTT thanked the Council for the kindly treatment he had received during the five years he had been a member. He had disagreed sometimes on matters of policy and principle, and the members had agreed to differ. Ile would look back upon those five years as the busiest and the happiest of his life. He thanked all the officials, from the Town Clerk down to the juniors, for the courtesy extended towards him and particularly Mr. Spinks, the Assistant Town Clerk, who had been his guide, philosopher and friend. Never on any single occasion had be been refused information he had asked for. The resolution showed that though the members of the Council might represent different politi- cal colours outside, they represented each other in the Council; and be hoped that spirit would long continue. For some years the Council meetings had been much quieter than they were when he first became a member. (Laughter.) lie did not think the Council was any worse for that-10 fact he thought it was better—and be hoped the Council would never go back to the bad old times of five or six years ago. He did not think there would be any reasons for such things to occur again. He hoped all the improvements the Council had in hand would be rapidly developed, and that Warring- ton would become in a few years time what Alderman Bennett, Canon Stevenson and all of them desired to see —a beautiful Warrington, really and indeed. (Hear, hear, and applause.) OLD AGE PENSIONS.

- --.—..—. TOWN COUNCIL TO BE THE LOCAL COMNIITTEE The TOWN CLERIC said he had received a circular from the Local Government Board with regard to the Old Ago Pensions Act of 1935, asking for the appoint- ment of a committee under the Act. They suggested that the appointment be made this month. He did not receive the circular until the Council summons had gone out, but he immediately took steps so that it could be dealt with that night. The Council could appoint themselves or themselves in part and outsiders in part as the committee, and they also could appoint any number of sub-committees. He did not know what the duties would be because the rules and regulations would have to made jointly by the Home Secretary and the Secretary of the Local Government Board, but he thought the matter could be dealt with by the Council constituting themselves as the committee and they could deal with the appointment of sub-committees later. It might be necessary for this year when there would be a large number of applications to appoint a sub-committee for every ward. Of course that was merely a suggestion. , Councillor EvaNs asked if the Council would be able ' to co-opt persons as members of the sub-committee. The TowN CLERK Certainly. The members of the sub-committee need not be members of the local pension committee.
Councillor Ev ass : They would have to submit their proceedings to the Council for approval. The Tows CLERK : Yes.
Alderman PlEnroisT formally moved that the Council be constituted the committee for the purposes of the Aid-age Pensions Act of 1908. Councillor PENIBERTON seconded.
Councillor STEEL asked whether the circnlar did .not suggest that members of Trades Councils and Friendly Societies should be members of the Pensions Committee.

The TOWN CLERK read an extract frona-tb-e—LOc7ll Government Board's circular which stated that the Council would no doubt be able to obtain from various sources, including local branches of trade unions or friendly or other societies, the names of Suitable and representative persons whose services might be utilized if desired on the Local Pension Committee or on the sub-committees. in p./ Alderman TINNION in supporting the resolution said it was advisable that they should proceed cautiously. At a future date, when they had a better idea of the regulations, it would be desirable to have the co-opera- tion of friendly societies, trade unionists, and anyone" who would be of assistance in getting the best possible results from the Act and administering it at as small a cost as they could. Councillor Srurr asked whether the Council could alter the constitution of the Pensions Committee, at some future time if thought necessary. The TOWN CLCEK said the Act and also regulations had not yet been printed, but he presumed they could do so. The resolution was then carried unanimously.

Cab Horse Dashes Into Window. An exciting scene was witnessed at Market-gate on Wednesday afternoon, a cabman and his fare having a narrow escaps from being killerl. John Oliver, of Dickenson-street, who is employed by Mr. Edward Connor, cab r rnprietor, Sankey-street, was driving Mr. 0. Withinshatv, of Peniceth, to the railway station, when the iii se took ft ight, and bolted through the main etrefts, which were thronged with market ye-pie. The animal eventually ran into the window - of the shop of Messrs. Smith and Walker. tailors, Marliet-gate, smashing the Tate glass. Mr. Withinshaw jrmnred out just before the imract, and escaped, hut the driver was I:itohed ff the box, and sustained injuries to tie Lead and arms. He was taken to the Infirmary where the wounds were dressed. The . horse was badly cat. PUBi IC TiFNEFIT UNDER TAR CLOCK FOR BEST POOTS IN LANCASHIRE—Advt. Throwing Stones at a Launch. At the Borough Police Coutt. on Monday before M. S. Wright (chairman), Couneillor Wilkinson. Messrs. H. Poberts, W. Robetts, T. W. Hayward, E .f. Guest, E. Wood, and J. Maginn, five boys named Walter Pronnerly, 29, Clifton-street, Edward Boswell, 238, Knutsford-road, Joseph Cross, 17. Oldham-street, George Howard, 3, Grove-street and William Henshall, 6, Barry-street, were charged with throwing stones in the Manchester Ship Canal at Latchford.- The eyid- eree showed that defendants stood on the Cantilever Bridge and threw at a passing launch. They were titling to drop the stones down the funnel and one missi:e narrowly missed the on-rer of the vessel.— Mr. Bev-cam-who represented the Canal Company, in reply to a suggestion from the Bench sail they would have notices printed warning the public about this offence. The chairman said the offenne was a serious one, but the boys would be dismissed on their parents under- taking to chastise them. Separation Order Granted. At the Borough Police Conrt on Tuesday, Ann J. Folcroft, residing at 62, Norris-street, was charged with being drunk in Panne-street. She was found lying across the footpath in a helpless c nclition, and she brought to the Police Station. Her husband , applied for a separation order on the ground that she was an habitual drunkard. He said be had been aortied by her for neatly four years. They had fow children, the oldest eight years and the youngest 18 months. She neglected her children, and spent all the money she could get on drink. She acted as if insane while tinder the influence of drinlc.—lnspector Cox, N.S.P.C.C., gave evidence to the effect that he had defendant under his observation for two years. Her Imsband obtained a separation order while they were living at Stockton Heath, but he went back to' her after a short time. The man was not to blame, as he was temperate and gave his wife sufficient money. —A. separation order was granted; allowing the 414-fendant 78 per week and leaving the children in custody of the husband.

TENNIS. CROWET AND GARDr:N R WRTESITEq.— J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge street, Warrington.—Advt. Shrewsbury Floral Fete. We would remind our readers that :the annual Shrewsbury floral fete which has the renutation of being the greatest fete in Gent Britain, will lie held on Wednesday and Thursday next. Prizes to the -value of .£1,200 are offered, and there will he 3,000 -exhibits staged in ten monster reargues. A special musical teat will be provided by the celebrated regimental bands of lI.M. floral Artillery (56 per- formers), H.ll. Coldstretim Guards (5(1 performers) and Ff.ll. %rm.:shire (53rd) Regiment. Forty separate Performances by the greatest artistes of the day will be given. There will be several balloon ascents, a horse-leapinc competition and numerous other attract- tions. Special excursions will he run from Warrington and all parts. Messrs. Adnitt and Nauntnn, of the Spar t, Shrewsbury, bare published a beautifully illustrated souvenir of the show, containing about 20 poges of photographs—the town, the show-ground, exhibits of grapes. flowers and vegetables, views of The Severn. Fze.— The price of the booklet is 3d. and in addition to the illustrations it contains a preface eivirg a resume of the origin of the s:lclety, with its income, and the donations it has given to various institutions and improvements in the town. Children's Camp. —Officers as Rescoars. An exciting incident, in which officere of the Warrington Children's Summer Camp acted as rescuers, occurred at Prestatyn on Satnrday after- noon. A contingent of boys in charge of their officers, were wading in the incoming tide, when it was observed that a servant and three little children were in difficulties' and unable to make the shore. 'The water had already filled in the deeper reaches in the sand banks. Do what she would the girl was "beaten back by the pressure and growing depth of water. .The father of the children made earnest efforts, but unfortunately, tried to make war at spots where the tide rendered it well-nigh impossible for him to help them. At this inneture Mr. Boardman, a young and active camp officer, managed to strike a . Point where he could get through, and he succeeded in bringing safely to their parent two little hope. Both the boys and their rescuer were well-nigh exhausted Mr. C. J. Newton bravely seconded Mr. Boardman's efforts, and got the elder child and the servant to a -place of safety. The second batch of b ,vs numbering 100, under the charge of Mr. Bamber, Mr. and Mrs. Turner and Mr. Farrar. arrived at Prestatyn last Saturday morning at 11-45 am. All were in excellent spirits Despite the fact that the weather has not been quite as favourable as during the previous weeks of the camp, a pleasant and healthful time has been spent. The children were excellently catered for Lv Mr. and Mrs. Whitney and Miss E. Bostock. Mrs. W. Turner acted as matron to the camp.

"Poor child!" said the Hussar kindly, "you mustn't be miserable. We shall always have the memory of our happiness." - "Ah, Tes ; the memory!" A cold comfort, thought Pero., who fancied memory as something grey, a haze covering all bright things, a grey heaven, a grey earth, grey roses ' • the voice of the nightingale sounding dim and distant, a mere shadow and veil of the present —a poor, .nnsubstantial substitute for all the radiance and joy encompassing her hitherto. The Hussar sighed. His blue eyes looked sal. These explanations were always very awkward, and he hated giving pain. Every brave man must. Peril was brave, too, in her primitive feminine fashi( n. She did not cry or complain, or reproach him ; she only sat quite still with a white face and quivering lips. She was like _some dumb stricken creature, patient in its uncomprehended misery. The'llussar would almost, rather she had cried out and scolded him like a virago. He could have borne it better. He was very sorry for her, but he was very sorry for himself, too. "These things are hard on a man. It is hard to leave a pretty little girl with fond grey eyes and a trusting. smile, when it irrans for long years, if not for ever. Of course it might not be for ever. But the chances were against their meeting any more, and if they did, who knows whether their feeling's might not have changed? She might no longer care, nor he. No, it was better to treat the parting as if it were for ever. The Hussar was gone. Pera sat alone in her garden. The shadows deepened till they looked quite dark and mysterious. The roses exhaled a sweeter odour, the evening dew moistened her feet,. but she sat on unheeding, a very cold, unconscious statue. Could it be possible? Was Fate really so cruel? Was he gone—gane for ever and aye? She must spend the rest of her existence, a very long one, perhaps, stretching out over numbers of years, alone! rem despaired. Life seems inter- minable when one is young. Then her dog, with alino3t human sympathy, climbed into her lap. Tha' silence of his young mistress, her quietude, so different from her usual lively laughing ways, exasperated him. Even dogs want gaiety and companionship around them. He proceeded to lick Pera's fingers,. he even sprang up and ventured to lick her cheek. He nestled into her arms, and curled himself against her bosom, a very cushion of softJur. Pent bent down. The dog's sympathy melted her hard regretful mood, a tear dropped on his faithful muzzle. "We are alone now, you and .1," she whispered, fondling him. "He is gone away and I cannot forget." The little dog wagged his tail, and seemed to understand.

Then the days dragged on slowly, long, weary days of solitude. Nothing happened. The curate still dropped in to tea pretty persistently, and the law student paid occasional visits. Yet Peva seemed to herself to be always alone. 'The world was such,a vast, cold place for one poor little girl, and there is a solitude of the heart that even society cannot fill. The curate visibly worshipped her, but none of the glamour of the warrior wrapped him round. His was no martial atray, no panoply of war, no trumpet sound of fame. An umbrella formed a bad substitute for the sword, and the jingle of spurs was ill represented by the pattering of indiarubber goloshes. No, his love- making did not progress, for Pera, even more strongly than ever, believed she could only marry a brave man. The curate was very busy. He lived among the realities of life. An epidemic raged in the village, and he had set himself to combat it. There were deaths and buryinga and distress and sorrow all around, and only the curate and the doctor to deal with them. The vicar, a rich man, who indulged in the luxury of a locum teases, 'was absent, locking after his health in Switzerland, so that no one thought it necessary to share the curate's responsibilities. He was free to toil, free to worry himself, free to go about with a bright countenance doing his best with words of comfort, and such giving of good things as he could manage from the slender stores at his disposal. He had a fair field for effort, and every facility for killing himself in his master's service. So lie worked night and day, grudging himself rest, snatching hasty meals. and sparing neither mind not body. When Nature asserted herself occasionally his hands drooped, and his faith faltered, as haplens sometimes even to saints and martyrs, he would turn to his ideal and think of the little maiden sitting in her rose- garden, the embodiment of rest and Leanly, till his courage returned, and he worked on again stead- fastly. One evening as he sat late at his books, seieng one of those brief moments for study, which were now so rare, he noticed a strange light in the sky. Alert add interested, he' opened the lattice and looked out. The night was very dark, but just over the fir trees a flare of red broke the pitchy blackness. In the air rose a smell of burning. The curate dashed the lattice to. "A fire!' he said to himself, pitching on his goat and forgetting the goloshes and umbrella. "A fire! I wonder where it is." On the way down he met some cf the villagers bent on the seine errand as himself. "What is it—a farmstead, a rick? What is it ?" he queried hastily. ••• "It be the ou.ld Manor Cottage," one rustic answered. The curate staegered in his hasty flight. The Manor Cottage, the home where his lady-love liver:: Fear lent him new wings. Almost the first on the ground he saw furious flames leaping and curling ronmi the eaves and the chimneys. The crackle of red-hot timber fell on his ear, and the air choked him, heavy-laden with the smell of smoke and cinders. The curate looked round. Servants had done what they could ; buckets were brought and emptied, each man busily lent a hand. "And the lady ? " the curate, faint at heart with terror, asked. "Is she safe? " At that moment a girl clad in white, her hair unbound, appeared at the window. She made as though to fling herself out." "Don't jemp!" the bystanders cried; "wait— wait—a ladder! Somebody brine a ladder!" As usual in such cases, no ladder could be found. The crowd hesitated and looked at one another doubtfully; every/moment more thrilling, the heat waxing intensely A shiver ran over the

"Would you have saved anybody, any other person but me?" asked Pers presentiv. The curate hesitated. "I hope so," he answered truthfully. "But you are not sure?" cried the girl triumphantly. "It was we you saved—only me. Then, that is love," she added softly. "I suppose so," said the•curate; "but why talk of these things? Let us rather consider the plans of the new house, which you must shortly rebuild." "I shall not rebuild it—at least not like that," raid Pera decisively; "that part of my life is over, and I must have a new houte, newly-planned, to live my new life in. Papa was a scholar, a recluse ; he built a house for solitude, for silent sork, for himself. I am going to have a new house, a house full of joy and laughter, and the Merry cries of children. lam not going to read my life-story in books, but in the great big, busy world, and in the hearts of others. lam going to work, for the future, and not to dream. "That is well," said the curate ; "and what shall be your work ?2' "To forget myself) to bring smiles to the sad faces, joy to the poor in heart, happiness to the careworn, health to the sick, rest to the toiling." "A ministering angel!" said he. • "No, only a far-off humble follower in the steps of the curate."

"Ah I And you think that yill make you happy t" "I know it, " said she. "Thep my occupation will be gone; there is not room in the village for two workers." "I shall only be your aide-de-camp." "And suppose I will not have you as my airie- r:lc-camp? Suppose I could not endure the tantalus torture? Suppose I could not bear to breathe the atmosphere of your sweetness all day long? Suppose it cloyed and killed me, and took away my strength? Suppose I was a coward, and ran away from .temptation ? ".

"Then we should have to make other arrange- ments," answered Perm decidedly. *. Her hand lay on the table, fingering the roses in the bowl. Those little thin fingers had once curled round the curate's neck, lie had not forgotten their soft clinging, lie yearned to touch them once more, to take them again into his rough man's hand and cover them with kisses. But he did not dare ; the curate was really at heart a coward. "What are you thinking of ? " Pero, said with a smile. Stung to madness, the curate answered: "I am thinking of your hand." "What of it?" and she held it out to him with a saucy gesture. . . - - - -
The curate seized it greedily, and the kisses he had so long restrained fell on it thick and fast. . . _

"The hand is the key to the heart," said Pera, with one of her pretty pouting smiles. "Then I will take your heart," cried the curate desperately, as he pressed his lips to hers. "You will marry me now?" he asked anxiously. "Did I not always say I could only marry a brave man?"

And I am brave in your eyes ? " !Pen. nodded, and motioned him to sit beside her. :"You remember the,sundial's motto," she asked: "` To-day for me, to-morrow for you '? " The curate said nothing, but he kissed her again. [Tun ESD.

" CANADIAN " IDEAL HOLIDAY. If I had plenty of money, I should like to go abroad for a few months to Canada, during the winter season. I should have a real good game at sledging and skating and tobogganing, for I am so fond of games. I should pay a visit to the great lakes and the Niagara Falls, sl.oot the Rapids, and so on. I might visit Ottawa, the capital. But, in the midst of all my enjoyments, if I had a heavy purse, I must not forget those who are in need of help, and give a helping hand to the hospitals, and so bring a ray of sun into some poor sufferer's heart. Thus remembering the wOrds, "Whatso- ever ye do unto one of these little ones ye do it -to Me." W. RIISUBY.
AN IDEAL HOLIDAY. -

First, to take train from London to one of the well-known watering-places of Wales, such as Aberystwyth. This is one of the best places I think for a good holiday. Besides being nice and quiet, the health rate is one of the best in England. A week spent in this town, and plenty of money to spend, I believe is as good a holiday as any one could wish for. From this town one could take a trip to Llandudno, another favourite Welsh pleasure resort. dt course, we all know the Welsh language is quite different from our native language, but there are many English hotels in Wales where our native language is spoken. Many of us have izot seen mountains in England, but a trip to the East of Wales will bring us to the Cambrian tangs of mountains. WILLIE JOHNSON.
-+-- AN IDEAL HOLIDAY.

I should take a ticket for Ilfracombe, and there spend a day. From Ilfracombe I should go to Exeter, and from there book for London. I should like to spend about nine days in Lon- don. The last place in London I should go to would be one of the docks. I stould inquire if there were any steamers going to Calais. When I had got all the particulars of the ships sailing, I should pick out the one most com- fortable, and embark on it. When the ship had reached Calais, I should take a ticket for Paris at one of the railway stations. I should then spend the remaining days in surveying France, which we hear so much about. I should get back to London the same way I came, and there take a through ticket to Bideford. After spending my month's holiday, I am sure I should be able to work for another twelve months on the strength of it.
HARRY Copp.
HOW I -SHOULD LIKE 'TO SPEND MY
SUMMER HOLIDAYS.
AL MONTH'S HOLIDAY. FaexcE, &c.

The first visit I should make would be lo fTi city of London, where I should spend a few days. After being in London, I should visit France. In France I should go to Paris, where I should visit the beautiful Cathedral of Notre Dame. I should also go to Lyons and Mar- seilles. At all the towns I visited I should try to get an opportunity of going into the factories where the various manufactures- are carried on. After spending some time in France, I should go to the beautiful mountainous country of Switzerland, which is almost entirely covered by the Alps. Switzerland is known as the "Playground of Europe." In Switzerland I should visit the picturesque lakes, valleys, glaciers, and chief towns. My next proceeding would be to go to,ltaly; there I should visit the volcanic mountains of Vseervius and Etna, and the towns of Rome, Florence, and Naples.. My final visit would be to Spain and Portugal, visiting the towns of Madrid, Valencia, Seville, Lisbon, Oporto, and the key to the Mediter- ranean—Gibraltar. IDA Bow.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
Mr, Allan Wilkie's Shakespearean Company.

Mr. Allan Wilkie and his talented Shakespearean ! Company hold a high place in the estimation of War- ! rington theatre-goers and their return visit to the Royal Court Theatre this week has been warmly welcomed. Such an admirable repertoire as this company presents could not fail to be a strong attrac- tion and each play has been followed with interest and appreciation by a large audience. Mr. Wilkie has risen to the front rank of tragedians and his Shakes- pearean productions are characterized by a forcefulness and originality which compel attention. The week's programme was fittingly inaugurated with , " The Merchant of Venice "—that gem of poetic beauty and dramatic skill which appeals as strongly as ever to lovers of Shakespeare. Mr. Wilkie's striking delineation of Shylock held the audience spell-bound. It was impressive in its force and intensity, but we thought some of his outbursts of fury were a little too frenzied. He was seen at his best in ! the trial scene where after turning a deaf ear to all appeals for mercy, he was almost stupefied with ' mortification at the unexpected turn of the scales against him, and could only stagger speechless from the Court. Mr. Wilkie's; clever portrayal met with general approbation and he had many enthusiastic !" calls." Miss Carrie Baillie achieved a triumph as Portia. She gave an ideal rendering of a charming part, and in the piquant passages which caused such ! great amusement as well as in the touching plea for ! mercy in the trial scene, she acted with a naturalness and power which delighted all. Mr. Alexander Marsh, as the passionate 13assanio, had a part which suited him admirably and he did full justice to it. Mr. John Paley won high opinions for a capital study of Antonio; Mr. Ernest Digges did well as Lorenzo; Miss Maud Gill was a winsome Jessica, and \Miss Mildred Surrey was a vivacious Nerissa. A word of praise is due to Mr. Sinclair Neill who as Prince of Morocco infused great fervour into his acting in the casket scene. Mr. lan Fleming as Lancelot Gobbo was irresistibly amusing, and the scene in which he and Old Gobfio (Mr. P. J. Fay) were associated was one of the most popular incidents of the comedy. All the other parts were in capable hands and the play was attractively mounted. On Tuesday evening " Othello " was presented with great success. Mr. Wilkie at once gripped the audience by his vigorous and powerful interpretation of the title Kole, while Miss Carrie Baillie won all hearts as Desdernona. Mr. Alexander Marsh's finished study of the unenviable part of lago was worthy of ill praise. On Wednesday evening the attraction was Colley Cibber's version of "Richard 111 ," Ur. Wilkie adding to his laurels by a brilliant performance as the unscrupulous King. Miss Baillie also did admirably as Lady Anne. . On Thursday Shakespeare's ever-popular tragedy "Romeo and Juliet " was enacted before a large audience. The leading characters of the two lovers were most dramatically impersonated by Mr. Alexander Marsh and Miss Carrie Baillie supported as they were by Mr. Allan Wilkie in the part of Friar Lawrence and an able body of helpers who filled the numerous cast. The intensity of feeling and dramatic power shown alike by Mr. Marsh and Miss Baillie deeply moved the audience and there were numerous aud hearty calls before the curtain.

La'st evening a special double prngramme was sub- mitted. It opened with " The Sleigh Bells," Mr. Wilkies's acting as " Mathias " being most weird and gelding the tense interest of the audience. The ever- popular " David Garrick " followed, Mr. Alexander Marsh doing full justice to the title part. To-night "Hamlet " should draw a crowded house. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

div.head: C.E.T.S. RESCUE AND PREVENTIVE WORK.
div.p: C.E.T.S. RESCUE AND PREVENTIVE WORK.

During the summer months when much of the philan- thropic work that is carried on during the winter is -either discontinued altogether or considerably diminished the Police Court Missionaries continue to work at full nressure. It was recently stated by a Member of Parliament that the Diocesan Branch of the C.E.T.S. has " permanent officials who devote the whole of their time in speaking about temperance or against the trade." This if, certainly not the case with the missionaries, as the following record of some of the work which they did in July will show. In the police courts and bridevrells they had no fewer than 1352 con- versations with those whom they were trying to influence for good. They visited 100 cases from the courts and interviewed 369 discharged prisoners who called on them either at their homes or at the Society's offices. In addition to the f roe breakfasts given at the Mission Room, they supplied 99 persons with food and 41 with clothing and wrote 257 letters in order to help those who were in need. It is impossible to tabulate the results of their work, but there is no doubt whatever that it is on right lines and that it must be productive of good.

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday August 15, 1908.

Perhaps the flirtation had gone deeper than he meant. Perhaps she would be unhappy. Her grey eyes seemed latterly to hold a new wealth of tender- ness within their depths. But then, it could not be helped—that was the life of a soldier, to love and to ride away. The hour had come for him to ride away. They wandered from the rose garden to the tawn below, flanked by the old grey wall over which climoed a tangled mass Of fragrant white roses. In the distance a nightingale began ti sing, and Pens stood still and listened. The girl's face pointed upwards. On it was an expression of divine content. The Hussar saw it and shivered. He would rather have faced the fire of the enemy than that expression of divine content. "Pera," he said, taking her hand. ra did not withdraw it; but she cast on him a look brimming over with tenderness. The Hussar knew it well. He had seen that look on other wenien:s fsces before.. "What has happened'? " she cried, when he stopped, abashed. lam fright en ed, somet hi ng has happened. I see it in your face—you do not love me! _ _ _ . .

"Indeed I love you too well, my dear little girl; too well for my peace of mind—too well for our banpiness. Be brave, Pera." "Be br vet" the poor Child muttered, remember- ing her declaration that she could only marry a brave man. "Must women, then, be brave I 1 can be brut w'.th you always." Ile hell her close to him, her cheeks touched his lips, their hands were interlaced—it was easier to speak so. "Pera, be brave!" He repeated the words. "With you, my king, always., always," she answered meekly. "Not with nv, but without me." He thrust out the wolds somehow half-inarticulately, till he saw her cheek blanch, and felt her limbs totter; then, placing her tenderly on the stone-seat, he took her two hands in his. 'Pers., listen! You would not love me if I were a coward. I tmust do my duty; I must leave you. We are ordered abroad imme- diately. The news only came to-day." "For ever?" Pero questioned feebly. "Who can tell? I soldier carries his life in his hands. I may not return." "But if you do?" "Ah, Perm. it does not do to plan out o'he's future. 1 wish to leave you free."
"But I may go on thinking of you, my king, my soldier ? The Hussar hit his moustache."
"Yes, think of me, as I shall of you, with faithfulness and truth."'
"With faithfulness and truth. Mug I be.free ? I would rither not." _ _

- "And I would rather. Of course I love you dearly, but--" Pert, alast knew the meaning of that hut, the little syllable that extinguiehed for her all hope and joy, and the happy dream that had made life beautiful. •

bystanders, for clouds of smoke almost jbsctzte d the trembling white figure at the window. Then might be seen a man, his body wound round with a strong rope, who climbed up by the verandah, aiding himself, with hands and feet, by out- standing buttress, nail, waterpipe, crevice, or foot- hold of any sort. Like neat, with swiftness and surety, he climbed, to the astonishment of the yokels, not one of whom wottla have dared to perform the feat.

When he reached the window the girl fell almost hysterically weeping into his arms. Quietly unwinding the rope from his body he fastened it to the 'window-sill and proceeded again to descend, this time carefully with the girl clasped in his arms. As he reached • the ground a great cheer went up from the applauding multitude to whom deeds of courage never appealed in vain. The fire being at last extinguished, and all that could be saved by the combined efforts of the fire- men—now tardily arrived—and the willing volunteers, the curate, the hero of the hour, went home to bed, bruised, weary, but joyful'at heart. "How glad I am, I thought of being a sailor once," he reflected, 'and learnt to climb. ' Those birds' nests I robbed as a boy were not wasted; they taught me skill and prudence." \ Pera was safe ; he had left her in the care of the old servant, pale but unharmed. Safe! safe! the joy bells rang in his heart. If she had perished he would, at least, have perished with her. But she was not dead, she Was alive and well, and he had saved her. God was very merciful! The curate fell asleep and dreamt that he was walking over red-hot plough Shares, which burnt him dreadfully. Yet he cared nothing for the pain, for away in the distance, radiantly beautiful, in her white robes stood Pera, beckoning to him kindly, and smiling an angelic smile of wklcome..

Again the curate sat at tea with Pera, no longer in her own sweet rose-garden, all blackened and trampled down and strewn with debris after the Ere, but in a cosy little room in the empty Vicarage, which she had gladly accepted in her time of distress and homelessness. •

She lay on the sofa, still somewhat white and shattered in nerve from the effects of her recent danger. The curate looked much as usual, sitting with his faithful umbrella propped beside him. Pera raised herself, leaning on her elbow. "They tell me it was you that saved me. I remember nothing. It was all a horrible, dream. I don't believe I even- thanked you." "I want no thanks. I only did my duty." "Do you mean to say you are in the habit of saving people in burning houses?" , "No; lam not so vain. I don't think I ever did anything Of the sort before." "But you would, I'm sure," said Pera, gazing steadfastly at him, "you would.; I believe there is something daring and quixotic in your nature." "Hardly," the curate smiled "Ain I not only a man of peace?" "There are men of peace and men of peace," mused Pera. "Yours is a fighting nature; you love danger." "I simply never think of it," the curate replied. "And that is the secret of courage," said the girl on the sofa, lying back on her cushions.

The curate looked at her. He saw her always in his mind's eye,as on .that dreadful night. The tangled masses of her long brown hair, hanging over his shoulder, falling across his mouth, blinding his eyes, the litCe bare feet dangling helplessly, ,and the warm young body clothed only in the flimsy nightdress, pressed against his heart, nestling on his bosom. She was pretty now, charming in the pensive delicacy of hoe*, new thoughtfulness ; but never would she be again the sweetheart of his dreams, in her appeling agony and self-abandon- ment.

Supposing my holiday to begin on August Ist, I should like to take a friend and go down to the Isle of Wight. I should stay at an hotel in Cowes, and there see the great regatta. I should go down to the sea every morning be- fore breakfast and have a good bath. I should go and see the Needles, and one day I should go in a ship to the Channel Islands. Before long, however, I am afraid I should want to go somewhere else. Therefore, I should fake very long railway journey into the mountains of Scotland, and stay at that most beautiful of all Scottish seaside towns, Oban. I should take a trip in a steamboat, and sail up that canal which derives its name from the old name for Scotland, "Caledonia." This canal was cut for hading purposes, but it is now very little used, except by holiday-makers. The town at the other end is Inverness. This is a very old Scottish town, and I should like to have a good look round it. I should then pay a visit to-the battlefield of Culloden, where once and for all the rising of the Highlanders, and,.with it, the last hope of the Jacobites, was crushed. I should next take a tour among the Grampians, of which Ben Nevis is the highest point. Oh, how jolly it would be to climb up the steep, rocky sides of the mountains, thousands of feet above the level al the sea I should next pay a visit to Lockleven Castle, in which Mary Queen of Scots was imprisoned after the battle of Carberry, and from which, with the aid of friends, she made her escape. I should then go to the Island of liewes, in the Outer Hebrides, and stay there foe a week or so. Then I should take ship and sail round by the north and east coasts of Scotland home again. I think this will complete my holiday, so I will say, -"Good-bye," until next summer. W. C. FAULKNER.
IT NEVER FAILS.
"Do you see that gentleman sitting oppo- site?" said one man in the train to his neigh- bour. yes."

"I'll bet anything you like I can make him pull his watch out of hie pocket and consult the time, without saying A word to him." "'All right," said his .friend,, "I'll bet the best cigar to be had youilon't." - And the speaker proceeded to try his experi- ment. He waited a few moments until the glance of the man referred to fell on him, and then, with much deliberation, drew forth his watch and looked at it. The man saw the movement, and instantly lifted his own watch from his vest pocket. "It never fails," said the successful experi- menter, as they proceeded to secure the cigars. "Look at your own watch,. and you'll find it's as catching as yawning. Try it yourself."

Mrs. Sarah Kay, who lives next door to prisoner, said that on Thursday night last she was going home uhen she was met by Mrs. Lucas who was talking to another woman. Mrs. Lucas made an offensive remark to her, and some words followed, upon which she went into her yard, caught up a bottle and hurled it at Mrs. Ray. lhe bottle struck her on the forehead and broke, inflict- ing extensive wounds one over two inches long. Dr. Graham afterwards abstracted five pieces of glass from the woman's bead. Evidence corroborating complain- ant's statement was given, and prisoner admitted throw- ing the bottle.—The magistrates said that prisoner might easily have killed the woman. She must go to gaol for three months' hard labour.

• Dear Uncle Ned,—l am just going to tell you how I should like to spend rriz month's holi- day. First, I should like to have a large sum of money, then I would go to Basingstoke to see my aunt and cousins. Then I should like' to go to Southsea and have.a goat ride, because it is such jolly fun; and then to Southampton to see all the large ships coming in and going out. Then I should go to London to see all those :mad places that I hear and read so much about, and go out for a sail on the river Thames, and buy some of those nice things I should see in the shops, such as chocolate, sweets, cake; and when I got tired of walking, jump into a tram and drive to some of the beautiful parks, and then have a nice long ride in the train back home again. Then, if I had any time left, I should go to Westward Ho! and lie on the pebbles and watch the waves tossing about. DAISY' Cops'.

The head waiter ,at the Highland Hotel was purple with rage. "The dirty skinflint," he cried; "the cheese- paring, swindling Yankee! " "What's the matter, John?" asked the manager.

"Matter," snorted John; " matter! why, that long American chap that was here all last month. Before he went away he told me he'd run short of ready money, but as soon as ha got up to London he'd send me a piece of paper that would make me smile." " Well? " said the manager. "It's come," continued the infuriated napkin wielder.
"That's all right," said the other; "what is it—a fiver?" _

—+_— HE DIDN'T SEE IT EITHER. A showman was making a great fuss at the front of his exhibition of the wonders he had inside. A man standing in the crowd with a little toy beside him, cried out:— "I'll bet you 5e.-you cannot let me see a lion."

"Done," said the showman, eagerly; "put down your money." The man placed ss. in the hand of a by- stander, and the showman did the same. "Now walk this way," said the showman, - "and I'll soon convince you. There you are," said he, triumphantly; "look in the corner at that beautiful Numidian lion." "I don't see any," responded the other. "What's the matter with you?" •asked the showman.
"I'm blind," was the grinning reply, and in a few minutes the blind man pocketed the two five-shilling pieces, and went away.

MOTOR CAR AND CYCLE REDULATIONS. .Esa one must be registered with the council of n county or county borough, the fee being .C 1 for a motor car, and ss. for a motor cycle. A registered number is assigned to each, which it is an offence not to keep affixed when driving. Each driver must passers a license, costing 55., to be renewed every 12 months, and obtainable from the county authorities, which may he endomed or suspended for reckless driving or certain other offences. The highest speed at which a car may be driven on the public hzgliwn3s is '.20 miles an hour, which is reduced to 10 miles under special local regula- tions. It is an offence under the Motor Car Act (1903), to drive a car in such a way on a public highway as to be dangerous to the public, hiving regard to all the circumstances of the case. .

In the event of an accident to any person due to presence of the motor car on the road, the driver must supply his name and address, and tbe owner and number of the car, under heavy penal- ties. The driver must produce his licence at the request of a police constable.
The Examiner, Saturday August 15, 1908.

div.head: TERRITORIALS.
div.p: THE TERRITORIALS.
South Lancashires Return from Camp.

The camp of the South Lancashire Brigade at Knockaloe, Peel, came to an end on Sunday, and,despite the hard work—how very hard it was only these who shared in the trniuing can rightly tell—the memories it will leave are on the whole exceedingly pleasant. Immediately reveille MILS sounded on Sunday morning the canvas town was slicer.° of the ctrecst animation There were tents to le struck, kits to pack, stores to. be returned, end it may here be said that the men set about the work with that alacrity which Las distinguished all ranks from the beginning to the end of the training. The first corps to leave Knockaloe was the 9th Kings, which embarked in the Mons and cast off from Peel Pier prompt to the time arrangtd. The Liverpool Scottish followed in the Dougiss, and the two battalions of the South Lancashire Regiment brought up the rear in the Queen Victoria. Curiously enough, the order of arrival of the three boats at Liverpool was exactly reversed, the passage of the Moue being considerably lengthened, owing to her having to call at Ramsey to ' pick up a detachment of the Royal North Lancashiie Regiment. Gathered at the pierhead to welcome home the troops was a huge crowd. The three boats arrived within a quarter of an hour of eac'i other, end as the I various battalions, headed by their respective bands, I swung briskly along the Prince's Parade the splendid effects of the fortnight's training was strikingly apparent. The programme of work in the first camp of the South Lancashire Brigade under the new order of things was of the stiffest. Day after day for ton to twelve hours at a stretch the troops bad to tramp ow r the dusty roads, to scramble perspiringly up the rugged slop-a, or wade wearily through the exasperating bogs, and they ever stuck to it with a grim determination to see the thing through to the end. On Bank Holiday, food. less for many hours under a scorching sun, a numter of them had to knock under; but, taking it all in all, the " casualties " during the operations were very few indeed. This weather was magnificent from beginning to end of the training. As a matter of fact, a few refreshing showers—there were none to speak of during the fortnight—would have been gladly welcome. It remains to add that not only the brigadier, bet also Sir Charles Burnett and other distinguished officers who visited Knockaloe during the training, were one and all delighted with the conduct of the men? with the hiqh state of discipline maintained, and with the splendid progress made in the march towards efficiency.

div.head: RETURN TO WARRINGTON.
div.p: RETURN TO WARRINGTON.

. TLe Warrington Territorials reached home about 7.15 on Sundey evening end had a rousing reception. It was a struggle to reach the Drill Ilan through the thronged streets, many hands being outstretched to Welcome home the bronzed and healthy-looking soldiers. The general opinion was that Peel was the most successful camp ever held, and if Colonel Faircluugh is favoured with equally good weather next sear he may look forward to seeing many of his men again in camp for the whole fortnight's training. It is reported that the next camp will be at the Curragh in Ireland.

Councillor Stott Testimonial F und. Sir,—Will you itindly allow me through the medium of your paper to remind all intending subscribers to the above Fund, that the Fund will close on August 20th; and I suggest they send their contribution to ma rot later than 12 noon on that date. The presentation will take place on above date at 9.0 p.m. at a social, particulars of which are in your advertisement columns. Thanking you—l remain yours, Scc., JO,3IIPH PODAOII,E, Jun. lion. 8, Flylands-street.

-- Sir,—Will you kindly permit me briefly, rig a workm,„, admirer, through the medium of your influential columns to express my sincere regret at the decision of Councillor Stott, J.P., to take his departute to another continent—to carve out a new career. I think the regret is general. No dissentient voice will break in upon the tribute of admiration, in which opponents, I am sure, will cordially join with friends to pay to Mr. Stott for his courage, his unswerving purpose, his laborious work for Trades Unionism, and his efforts to alleviate the condition of the workers. Like one of Mr. Browning's earlier heroes he has been "ever a fighter " for what appealed to his conscience as justice, tutth and right. I have watched his work in the Council and I have particularly admired his strenuous efforts to secure direct employment in the painting of the market, the recognition of trade union wage in Corporation contracts, 2.5. minimum for Corporation employees, and last but not least, the municipalization of the coal supply. The "Examiner" has occasionally paid a compliment to his labours, as the quotations under will go to prove. Referring to Councillor Stott's public criticism of the Medical Officer's Report and the Town Council's apathy, the " Examiner " said: "Councillor Stott is taking a part which does him credit as a svorkingman representative, and we hope his effarts in this direction will result in the lot of the poor man's family being made healthier and happier. (20th August, 1904.) "By the introduction of his (Councillor Stott's) omnibus motion relating to the letting of contracts by the Corporation, he has done excellent spice for the Trade Unionist cause. Councillor Stott's motion will make for fairer dealing between employer and employed. (10th September, 1901.) "We have it on the authority of Alderman Roberts that the painting of the market was never so well done as it is being done now. This is a valuable testimonial for the system of employing skilled labour direct, and Councillor Stott must feel gratified at the success of his scheme. It has found employment for the unemployed, and givensatiS- faction to the employer." (10th March, 1900.) lam sure your readers will join with me in wishing Fred Stott " God speed" in his journey, and happiness ttnd prosperity in his new home.—Yours etc., G ASWO R KER.
kman

div.p: TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL.
Farewell to Councillor Stott. THE WAGES OF POSTMEN.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and , Labour Council was held at the I.L.P. rooms, Friars' Green House, on Tuesday evening, Mr. J. Moorfield presiding over a good attendance, which included the Secretary (Mr. E. Plinston). POSTMEN'S WAGES. The SECRETARY said he forwarded copies of the Council's resolution on this subject to the Postmaster General, the local members of Parliament and to the Secretary of the Labour Party. He received replies from Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P.. and the Secretary of the Labour Party stating that the matter would have their immediate attention. Members would have noticed that the question had been raised in the House. On behalf of the Postmaster General, the ,following reply was read Sir. In reference to your letter forwarding the resolution of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council,l am desired by Mr. Sydney Buxton to call your attention to the Parliamentary return No. 2041 entitled Post Office changes in wages etc.' You will find fully stated in that document tie's principles upon which the scales of wages for Warrington Post Office servants were fixed. Yours truly, 11. D. DENMAN." He had not received any reply from Mr. A. J. King, M.P. Mr. DAVIES. one of the postmen's delegates, said the! latest intimation they had on the subject was that they I must go into the cost of living, and if they could show I any great variation between the cost in 1905 and at the present time, the Postmaster General would consider it. Mr. T. Swivel said that when they read the Post Office returns and saw what a large profit was made they ; would all agree that wages should not be reduced. It I showed them that if the Government took over other great works labour would lose by it. It behoved the Trades Council to stand by the postmen and agitate for an advance instead of a reduction. Mr. HALEY said the communication from the! Postmaster General did not take them any " forrader." He was assured by Mr. Seddon that the Labour party had the matter seriously in hand and would not let it drop until something has been done in the way of removing this obnoxious order. He moved that the Executive Committee be instructed to draw up a petition on the question to he signed by the trade unionists of Warrington. Mr. Sea ITII seconded. Mr. DELANEY said he thought they ought also to consider the case of the telegraph boys who on reaching the age when the Government no longer needed them were turned adrift. The SECRETATLY read a letter from the local branch of the Postmen's Federation tendering their hest thanks to the Trades Council for its eflorts on their behalf. The resolution was carried. LABOUR REPRESENT tTION. The SECRETARY said he was issuing a circular to the branches directing their attention to the importance of direct labour representation upon municipal bodies. The Trades Council, he pointed out, was desirous of Cnntesting at least one seat at the forthcoming munici- pal elections and the cash necessary for the purpose would be equivalent to 31. per head of the affiliated membership. A letter was read from the Postmen's Federation stating that they unanimously recommended that a candidate be brought forward to take the place of Councillor Stott. EDUCATIONAL QUESTIONS. The Council then discussed the report on the work of the Education Committee presented at the last meeting by Mr. E. Plinston. Mr. Owes asked if the Education Committee had considered the question of the employment of married' women as teaehers. He understood there were 500 female teachers out of work in Manchester alone. Mr. PLINSTON said that whenever opportunity had arisen combatting the appointment of married women to positions in schools, he had always opposed such appointments. Ile believed that when women, whatever their positions, were taken by someone with the Inten- tion of keeping them, they ought to be so kept. There were several appointments in Warrington which had been held for a long period by married women. Only one appointment had been made by the Committee Permanently and that was in the case of a widow. He did not think anyone would object to that. He was strongly opposed to married women being appointed to permanent positions when so many qualified teachers were out of employment. Mr. PO DMORE said he believed a section of the Educa- tion Committee who were not workingmen were strongly in favour of raising the ago of exemption from school attendance to 14 years. There were thousands of cases in Warrington where the income of the bread winner was so low that it would boa great hardship for children to remain longer at school than the age of thirteen. Mr. Pr:Le:heels said the School Attendance Committee were almost entirely of opinion that power must be given to them to differentiate between the deserving ! and undeserving cases. Possibly a majority of the I Education Committee who knew very little about the I hardships and sufferings of the working classes would vote in favour of the age limit being raised. Beforehe (Mr. Plinston) would do so, under the present circum- stances, ha would not hold his position on the authority a week longer. The CH AIRM %.N asked what progress had been made towards the provision of meals for school children, as there would doubtless be a great deal of poverty during the coming winter. Mr. PLINSTON said a scheme had been drawn up but before it could be put into operation they had to see whether the public would voluntarily subscribe the necessary funds. If they would not—and he hoped nobody would subscribe a penny—they would have to report to the Board of Education who would approach the Town Council for the purpose of levying a half- penny rate. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE FEDERATION. Mr. HALEY presented a report of the proceedings at the half-yearly meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation of Trades and Labour Councils which was held at 'Manchester on July 25th. Letters from several affiliated Councils were read re Magisterial appoint- ments on the County Bench. After some considerable discussion, it was agreed that Councils send to the Secretary, names for submission to the County Authorities, the Executive Committee to decide upon the means to be adopted in furtherance of their aims. Not more than two names should be sent from any one Council. A letter was read from Bolton re Labour Part 7'9 Unemployed Workmen Bill. It was agreed that the Labour Party be requested to re-introduce their Bill during the next Session of Parliament, and Councils were requested to approach the Party with that end in

SOME OP THE EXHIBITS. The section devoted to heavy horses was the outstand- ing feature of the show and was well up to the high standard which we have become accustomed to expect. MT. James Gould, of Lynirn, was, as usual, prominent and almort swept the board. His Holme Lacy Starlight, a nine year old bay, was first for brood mares Nvith foal and also carried off the district champion cup, and a silver cup given by Mr. John Cosoa for the best shire brood mare in a district class. She is considered to bo one of the biggest and prettiest mares in the country and has a flee record of successes, being first at the recent Birkenhead show, and first at the Royal Lanca- shire in Manchester. Here foal Lym n Boss, which beat all competitors for colt foals, will make a typical stallion. lamna BOSS has only been shown three times, having gained two firsts at Birkenhead and a first at Manchester. Mr. Gould was not represented in the open class for filly foals, where ths first prize went to Messrs. J. and G. Dickinson, of Cark-in-Cartmel, with Cark Victress, a good big foal with plenty of flat bone and feather, but in the district class for mares without foal, Lymm Blossom, a good weighty mare, full of shire character and a wonderful mover, took first and also won the Shire Horse Society's medal for the second year in succession. This animal won the fifty guinea cup at Birkenhead and has been second in London twice and third once. Of the three-year-old geldings or fillies, Mr. A. C. Sparkes' " Oldfield Ploughman," a grand animal, which has taken first and championship at London, was first. Mr. Alfred Broome's Windmill Duchess,' which was second, won Sir Gilbert Greenall's cup and Mr. Stapleton Bretherton's prize. It is a fine weighty animal, standing over 17 hands. The Warring- ton Corporation had the satisfaction of winning first prize in the class for geldings of four years and upwards with " Nelson," a beautiful grey, which also carried off premier honours in the tradesmen's section for single heavy horse. Mr. Lewis Dodd's black filly " Rustic Gipsy Queen," which was first in the two year olds was one of the finest fillies in the show and if it were a shade bigger would be one of the best animals in the , country. Other prominent prize winners were: Mr. , Walter Cunningham, of Childwall, Liverpool • Mr. Richnrd.Clarke, of Heatley ; Mr, Benjamin Wright, of

Mr. PODZIORE, teen years, seconded and said the letter well expressed what was in their hearts. The Council undoubtedly owed its present position to Councillor Stott who had not spared himself to advance their cause. His departure would mean more to the Labour movement in Warring • ton than they at present realized. He (Mr. Podraore) did not regret Councillor Stott's departure for his own sake, as be was confident the journey across the sea and life in another clime would mean longer life to him than if he had stayed in 'Warrington. Eulogistic speeches were also made by Messrs. W Bullock, T. Plumb, G. Leach, T. Haley, J. Delaney and the Secretary. Mr. Plinston remarked that the glamour of the Council Chamber had not deterred Councillor Stott from walking in the straight path and he had also been undaunted by the criticisms hurled against him. The resolution was unanimously carried. Councillor &roll' in reply said he had been almost Overwhelmed by letters and words of appreciation of the work he had attempted to do during the past six or seven years. While ha was secretary of the Tradas Council his ambition was to get every trade union branch in Warrington affiliated with the Council. He did not accomplish that and he felt that when one came to consider the work that needed doing in Warrington, he had accomplished very little indeed. He only wished he merited half the good things that had been said about him not only by members of that Council but by men belonging to all political parties and of every social standing. He had been surprised to find that although members of the Council had disagreed with him so often at the last meeting of the General Purposes Committee they. joined in bearing testimony to his honesty and sincerity One alderman went so far as to say that there had never been a men in Warrington who had been such a good and true friend to the working classes as he (Conncillor Stott). He did not want any better testimony than that. Although he had received congratulations and appreciation from men in high positions in Warrington, he felt still more pleased to know that he had gained the respect and admiration of that class which he had tried to represent in the Town Council. He said dis- tinctly that if he were returned to the Council he should look after the interests of the l'iorking classes, because the interests of the other classes had been and were now being very well looked after. Alluding to his impending departure, Councillor Stott said he was compelled to leave Warrington as his employer had decided to remove his works to Birkenhead. If he bad not decided to go to New Zealand he would have had to remove to Birkenhead, and after the fullest consideration he came to the conclusion to try his fortune in that Colony. He was naturally leaving Warrington and especially the comrades with whom he had been associated with deep regret. He had no definite work to go to,but was taking the risk. He was satisfied that he was leaving with the good wishes of the majority of the workingcla.sses of Warrington and he did not think any man could desire a better recom- mendation to a Colony. The unity of labour was the hope of the world. Although he was leaving good staunch comrades in Warrington, he knew he would find Soc•ialists and trade unionists in New Zealand. He hoped he would be able to rest from public activities for some time because, without regretting in any way his work in Warrington, he could assure them that from the physical standpoint he had suffered to a great extent. Although he had been a Socialist and a mem- ber of the Independent Labour Party since the forma- tion of the Warrington branch he had never, while hold- ing an official position on the Trades Council, tried to his opinions down the throat of any delegate. . . .

Mobberley. The hunters made a remarkably fine display—in fact there was not a bad horse amongst them, and it was very difficult to award the prizes. In the open class for hunters to carry between 13st. and list. 71b., Mr. W. A. Sinspeon-Hinelscliffes's " Broadwood," an exceptionally fine brown gelding, which has won at the Royal, the Lancashire and the Yorshire, was first. Mr. Stokes was second with a beautiful mover in " Swallow," and Mr. William Gale's "Will of the Wisp," the first as a novice, was third. la the heavy weight class there was an exceptionally fine struggle, and after Sir Gilbert Greenell had been called in as referee, the first prize was awarded to Mr. Stoke's bay gelding Savant," a beautiful animal and a splendid mover, and the second to the same owner's well-known " Astral." In the heavy weight novice class the Duke of Westminsteis "Just Cause " won well. The " specials " for hinters went to Mr. James Ri3harlson, jun., of Sliddlewich, who took a Hunters' Improvement Society medal in district com- petition; and to Mr. ft. Needham, of Knntaford, who won the Bournphrey Cup for the best filly in three distinct classes. The hackney classes, which were limited to the dis- trict, were highly creditable, the bale being wonder- fully good and quite the feature of the section. They formed one of the prettiest sights seen in a ring for many a long day, and what must be borne in mind is that they were all locally bred. The premier award went to Mr. Alfred Smith'schestnut filly, which moves alLround and is well-nigh perfect in shape. The year- lings were a small class, Mr. Joshua Ball's colt " Southworth Fire King" coming out first. The harness classes were excellent. Much to the satisfac- tion of the spectators, Mr. Arthur J. Willett's " Fire Belle " was first in the novice mares or geldings under 111 hands, and Mr. Joshua Ball's " Southworth Belle " secured first position in the novice class over 141 hands. The open classes attracted some of the most notable animals in the Kingdom.," The classes for mares or geld- ings not exceeding 14 hands and exceeding 14 and under 15 hands were of such a superior character that the judges suggested to Sir Gilbert Greenall that an extra prize should be awarded in each, and he at once agreed. The first wiz° in the class not exceeding 14 hands went to Mr. Louis Winans' " Tissington Kit Kat" which comes from the Walton stud. The winner in the other classes was Mr. Walter Winans' " Londesborough " which has won at Olympia and other noted shows. The second horse—Mr. John Kerr's " Londwater Flourish "—did not settle well and therefore did not appear to advantage in the ring or the decision might possibly have been reversed. In the class for mares or geldin„es, 15 hands and over, Mr. NV. Winans' tied for the chief prize with Miss Ella Rose, of Sale, who had entered. Grand Vulcan' against her rival's Cokers Rosador. Silver medals of the Hackney Horse Society were awarded to Mr. A. L. , Goodson, of Knutsford, and Mr. Walter Winans. The classes for tradesmen's or tenant farmers' turn- outs were of considerable local interest and showed that the owners of horses in Warrington and district take a pride in their animals. Messrs. J. and J. , Blinston, Bridge-street were first in the class for light horses with their bay gelding " Grandee Ind." Mr. ' William Monks, Bridge-street, secured firs in the vanners or light lnrry horses with hie chestnnt gelding "Clovis." The Warrington Corporation's grey gelding " Nelson" was first of the single heavy horses (trades- • men), and Mr. R. L. Warburton's (Hatton) grey mare • " Rose " was first in the farmer's single heavy section.

force . opin.- He was prepared to stand by his Socialism andlioped he would always be a Socialist. He fully believed that if he had not been a Socialist, he would not have been able to accomplish the work he had done in Warrington. • He hoped that Council would go on and prosper. At one time ha had great hopes that a combination of Labour and Socialist forces in Warrington would result in something substantial, but they saw that the trade unionists of Warrington were not then prepared to back up their delegates. They must strive to convince the rank and tile of the trade union movement that if they were to achieve what thoy were aiming at they would have to take political action and join with all the forces of progress. If they would do that, there was nothing to prevent them ' getting anything within reason. He hoped the Society tto which he belonged would see the error of its way, ' and before long re-join that Council and instead of lagging behind, would lead the forward movement in Warrington for the emancipation of labour. He hoped the united labour movement in Warrington and through- out the world would continue to grow until the workers were getting a fairer share of the products of their labour. (Applause.) A special resolution was then passed recording appreciation of the work of Mrs. Stott. The proceedings closed with the singing of "Auld Lang Syne."

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

GARDEN PARTY.—Saturday last was a day w the members of the Wesleyan Men's Bible Cl9ss choir will always remember. The President (Mr. ( Parker) gave the members and wives a cordial in tion to a garden party at Penketh Lodge. The r arriving at 3.30 p.m. were warmly welcomed by and Mrs. Parker. During the afternoon gamet , tennis and croquet were indulged in and at five o'c the party, which numbered about 70, sat down first-class knife and fork tea. Afterwards ain cricket match was played between Mr. C. E. Par eleven and the Rev. E.J.Gawne's eleven. This caused amusement, Mr. Gawne's side winning by SG runs t The match over, all adjourned to the front of the h where the :Bible class choir rendered two antl which, in the twilight of the evening, bad a , charming effect. Mr. Herbert Plumpton conductec Mrs. C. E. Parker accompanied. Afterwards the E. J. Gawne moved a vote of thanks to Mr. and Parker for their hospitality. Mr. Davey-Smith seco and the vote was supported by Councillor Fred and Mr. Midwood. Mr. and Mrs. Parker respondec said it had been a pleasure to have the company. brought a most enjoyable function to a close at eight o'clock.
